modules.title: When does a promise become a contract?
modules.doctrine: Distinguishing proposal, acceptance, promise, consideration, agreement, contract, void agreement and voidable contract.
modules.mechanic: classify social, moral and commercial promises, then assemble the legal chain that converts one into a contract.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three promises arrive (a dinner invitation, a fee promised to a neighbour after she has already fixed the roof, a signed purchase order). The player drags each into the foundry and sees which sockets auto-fill and which stay empty. One decision only: which of the three is closest to enforceable, and which single missing socket separates the other two from a contract.
modules.lab: the player is a lawyer holding a promise their client wants enforced, and the promise is currently just words at a family lunch. They receive twelve Intervention Points and a list of purchasable facts, each priced: obtain a written note (2), procure part-payment (3), get the promisor to specify a requested act (4), have a third person perform at the promisor's request (3), register the instrument (5). Each purchase fills sockets but also raises the Pressure meter, because facts assembled after the event look manufactured. Claude plays opposing counsel with a simple policy: attack the cheapest-filled socket first, and if the Pressure meter is above six, plead that the arrangement was never intended to operate in law. The decision points are genuine trade-offs. Buying part-payment fills consideration cheaply but converts a gift narrative into a commercial one, which helps here and hurts in Module 21. Buying registration is expensive and only pays off if the player later pivots to the s 25(1) route, so spending early forecloses flexibility. The hardest decision is whether to fill the consideration socket at all or to argue that s 25 excuses it, because the two theories are mutually undermining: pleading both signals that neither is strong. Pressure escalates over three rounds as Claude introduces contrary evidence, and the failure mode is a player who fills every socket and loses anyway because the assembled chain reads as a reconstruction rather than a transaction.
modules.win_loss: Win by reaching a filled chain with Pressure at or below five. Lose instructively either by running out of Intervention Points with the consideration or agreement socket empty, or by over-buying and losing on intention, which teaches that enforceability is not the sum of purchased elements.
modules.build_notes: Implement the chain as an ordered array of eight status nodes, each with fillStrength (0 to 3) and a sourceFact reference. Enforceability resolves only if every node has fillStrength at least 1 and the s 10 gate passes. Pressure is a derived value: sum of (factCost x postDatedFlag). Opponent policy is a pure function selecting min-fillStrength node.

modules.title: Why should law enforce a private bargain?
modules.doctrine: Freedom and sanctity of contract against legality, public policy, procedural fairness and unequal contractual power.
modules.mechanic: act as a rule-maker and decide which bargains society should enforce; each choice changes trust, freedom and exploitation meters.
modules.authority: Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd v Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986) 3 SCC 156
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three bargains arrive (a moneylender's compounding loan, an employment rule permitting termination without reason, a neighbour's promise to babysit). The player decides which the courts will enforce and immediately sees each meter move. One reveal follows: the Brojo Nath choice between void and voidable, and why the Court chose void.
modules.lab: runs four legislative rounds. In each round the player writes or amends rules, and Claude then plays the regulated market: a bank, a platform and an employer that adopt the cheapest strategy the current rules permit. The physics is that no rule is neutral. Making unconscionable terms merely voidable keeps Freedom high but sends Docket Load through the roof and lets Exploitation climb, because each affected person must sue individually. Making them void protects the weak but Claude responds by moving the same terms into non-contractual instruments (policies, service rules, terms incorporated by reference), so the player must then decide whether to extend the rule and how far. The strategic tension is that every protective rule the player writes has a circumvention cost, and the player must decide whether to spend enforcement budget on detection or on broadening the rule's scope. Broadening catches circumvention but chills legitimate bargains and drops Freedom. Detection preserves Freedom but consumes budget that could have funded courts, raising Docket Load. Round three introduces a shock: a cross-border platform outside the player's enforcement reach, which tests whether the earlier rules were written as substantive prohibitions or as procedural requirements. Failure mode is a player who optimises a single meter and finds in round four that the jurisdiction has either become uninvestable or has quietly legalised exploitation.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending round four with no meter in its red band and budget remaining. Lose instructively by achieving a perfect Exploitation score through rules so broad that Freedom collapses, which teaches why courts developed public policy as a residual category rather than a general fairness power.
modules.build_notes: Meters are 0 to 100 with red bands below 25. Each rule is an object with scope, sanction (void, voidable, penalty), enforcementCost and detectionRate. The simulated market is a policy function selecting the lowest-cost strategy whose detection probability is under a threshold. Expose the market's reasoning after each round so the player can learn the circumvention logic.

modules.title: Was this arrangement meant to be legally binding?
modules.anchor: ICA ss 2(e), 2(h), 10; intention is case-law based
modules.doctrine: Objective intention in family, social and commercial arrangements; intention is not expressly stated as a separate ICA requirement.
modules.mechanic: inspect WhatsApp messages, payment records and surrounding conduct to decide whether a casual arrangement became legal.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player inspects a finished twelve-week trail (messages, UPI records, a shared expenses sheet) and answers one question, whether the arrangement crossed into law, then sees which three artefacts actually carried the weight and which were noise.
modules.lab: inverts it. The player now lives the twelve weeks forward, with a private goal drawn at the start: either keep the arrangement outside law so they can walk away in week ten, or push it inside law so they can sue. Crucially the other cousin, played by Claude, has an unknown goal, and both parties are emitting artefacts into the same record. Each week the player chooses one artefact to emit and one to suppress, subject to a realism constraint: suppressing a payment means not getting paid, and suppressing a written term means accepting ambiguity that may cut against them later. The physics is the objective test. The player's private intention has no effect on the Court Reading; only emitted artefacts count, which means the game punishes the player who thinks 'we both knew it was casual'. Escalation comes in weeks six and nine when a real dispute arises and one artefact must be emitted under pressure. The sharpest decision point is week eight: the other cousin proposes writing down the profit split. Accepting builds Formality, which serves the enforcement goal and wrecks the escape goal; refusing preserves deniability but drives Reliance up, and a high Reliance index with low Formality is the fact pattern in which Indian courts have most often found a binding arrangement anyway. Failure mode is a player who over-formalises early and is bound by week three, months before they wanted to be.
modules.win_loss: Win by hitting the private goal at week twelve. Lose instructively by achieving the opposite Court Reading, which reveals which specific artefact tipped it.
modules.build_notes: Artefacts carry formalityWeight and relianceWeight. Court Reading is a threshold function over the emitted set, with a documented rule that high reliance plus moderate formality tips to binding. Keep the function inspectable in the debrief so learners can see exactly which weights decided it. Flag in-app that intention is not an express ICA requirement.

modules.title: Is the transaction void, voidable, valid or subsequently void?
modules.doctrine: Different defects produce different legal statuses, affected parties and consequences.
modules.mechanic: new facts enter during the transaction and the learner must update its legal status at every stage.
modules.authority: Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur & Co, AIR 1954 SC 44
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four fact injections arrive in sequence (a misstatement discovered, a supervening export ban, a party's undue influence revealed, a further part-payment made) and the player updates the status bar after each. The reveal shows which injection changed the status and which merely changed who could act.
modules.lab: gives the player the option-holder's seat in a machinery supply contract, having just discovered a misrepresentation that makes the contract voidable at their option under s 19. The market price of the machinery is moving, and here is the engine of the game: avoidance is worth a lot when the market has fallen and nothing when it has risen, so the player is tempted to wait and see. But every act of performance after knowledge feeds the Affirmation counter, and once affirmation is complete the option is gone permanently. Claude plays the counterparty with a policy of pushing performance milestones at the player precisely to burn the option. Three further pressures make this rich. First, a s 56 event (a temporary import restriction) is dangled in round two, and the player must judge whether it merely makes performance harder or strikes at the root, because a genuine s 56 event makes the contract void for both sides and destroys the player's leverage entirely. Second, if the player avoids, s 64 requires them to restore benefits received, so avoidance is expensive and the player must compute whether they can afford it. Third, a third party acquires an interest in the goods midway, which in real transactions is what usually forecloses rescission. The failure mode is the player who holds the option too long waiting for a better price and discovers in round four that they have affirmed by conduct.
modules.win_loss: Win by exiting or affirming at the point of maximum value while the option is still legally alive. Lose instructively by losing the option through unwitting affirmation, or by avoiding at a moment when restoration under s 64 costs more than the contract was worth.
modules.build_notes: Status is an enum with legal transitions only; block illegal transitions and explain refusals. Affirmation is a counter incremented by any performance action taken after knowledgeFlag is set, with a documented threshold. Price series is deterministic per seed so replays are comparable.

modules.title: Can the Government be bound by an ordinary bargain?
modules.doctrine: Governmental contracting power, mandatory form, authority to execute and consequences of non-compliance.
modules.mechanic: guide a supplier through quotations, approvals and signatures without relying on an unauthorized official.
modules.authority: Mulamchand v State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1968 SC 1218; State of West Bengal v B K Mondal & Sons, AIR 1962 SC 779
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player inspects a completed file and identifies the single defective link (a Superintending Engineer signed in his own name). Then one decision: proceed with supply or halt. Both branches are shown with consequences.
modules.lab: puts the player in the supplier's chair with a working-capital clock. The department is in a hurry, an oral assurance has been given, and the formally executed agreement is stuck in approvals. Every week of delay costs the supplier money, and the department official (Claude) applies steady pressure with a policy of promising regularisation later and escalating urgency, never refusing outright. The physics is unforgiving: performance without a compliant art 299 instrument produces no enforceable contract, and the supplier's only route is s 70, which requires that the act was lawful, non-gratuitous, and that the Government enjoyed the benefit. The decisions are all about sequencing under cost. Should the supplier halt and lose the working-capital clock, or perform and build a restitution file? Building that file well is itself a set of moves: obtaining written acknowledgment of receipt, ensuring delivery is to the department rather than to an individual, avoiding any language suggesting the work was done gratuitously or as a favour, and keeping the claim framed as compensation for benefit taken rather than as damages for breach, because the two are legally distinct and pleading the wrong one wastes the claim. Round three introduces the officer's transfer, which removes the friendly interlocutor and tests whether the file the player built stands on its own. The failure mode that teaches most is the supplier who performs on an oral assurance, pleads breach of contract, and loses on art 299 without having pleaded s 70 in the alternative.
modules.win_loss: Win by recovering value for what was supplied while remaining solvent. Lose instructively by holding an unenforceable contract with a well-documented breach claim and no restitutionary pleading, which is the most common real-world failure in government contracting.
modules.build_notes: Model each stage as a signature object with signatoryRole, expressedInNameOfGovernor (boolean) and authorityDocument reference. Contract enforceability against the State resolves true only if all three conditions hold at the execution stage. Section 70 claim strength is a separate score built from acknowledgment artefacts, non-gratuitous flag and benefit evidence. Note the doctrinal split in the debrief.

modules.title: Is it an offer or merely an invitation?
modules.doctrine: Distinguishing proposals from advertisements, displays, auctions, catalogues and invitations for tenders.
modules.mechanic: inspect advertisements, price tags, auction notices and tender documents and predict who makes the legally operative offer.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: five real-world artefacts are presented and the player marks each as proposal or invitation, then sees the commercial consequence of getting it wrong (a mispriced online listing binding the seller to a thousand units).
modules.lab: is a design exercise with a mischief. The player runs a seasonal sale and wants maximum customer commitment with minimum seller commitment, which is the actual commercial goal behind almost every retail communication. They draft each of the five channels, and Claude then plays a hostile market: a bulk buyer who tries to accept the listing at the advertised price for the entire stock, a bargain hunter who tenders exact cash at the window display, and a tender participant who claims the notice was itself a proposal. Each attack targets a different drafting weakness. The trade-off that makes this a game rather than a classification drill is that every protective drafting move costs conversion. Adding 'subject to availability and confirmation' keeps the trigger with the seller but reduces customer trust and, in the auction channel, reduces bids. Stating a fixed price with no reservation maximises conversion but converts the listing into something a court may read as a proposal, especially where stock is stated and the language is committal. The auction channel adds a second layer, because the auctioneer's call for bids is an invitation, each bid a proposal, and the fall of the hammer the acceptance, so the player must decide whether to reserve the right to withdraw and thereby depress bidding. Round three introduces a pricing error, which is the classic stress test: the player discovers a listing at one tenth of cost with two hundred pending customer actions, and must determine, channel by channel, how many of those actions were acceptances they are now bound by.
modules.win_loss: Win by clearing the season with revenue above target and Exposure below the ruin threshold when the pricing error hits. Lose instructively by drafting so defensively that conversion collapses, or by leaving one channel committal and being bound on the mispriced item.
modules.build_notes: Each channel is an object with commitmentLanguage (enum), stockStated (boolean), rightsReserved (boolean), priceDescribed (enum). A classifier function returns proposal or invitation with the reasons exposed. Conversion is inversely weighted to protective flags so the trade-off is real. The pricing error event fires at a fixed turn.

modules.title: Can a promise be made to the whole world?
modules.doctrine: General, unilateral and standing offers; acceptance through performance.
modules.mechanic: decide whether to act on public rewards and standing offers while conditions and availability change.
modules.authority: Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt, (1913) ILR 35 All 489
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three claimants arrive and the player decides which have accepted. One performed the act in full, one performed most of it after the offer was withdrawn from the company website, one performed a different act that achieved the same result. The reveal turns on s 8 and on what counts as performance of the conditions.
modules.lab: is a liability-management game under a budget. The company's board has capped total exposure, and the player must bring all three promises to a close without incurring a claim they cannot pay. The core physics is that revocation of a general offer must reach at least as far as the promise did, so a promise blasted across national television cannot be quietly withdrawn from a webpage. The Publicity Reach figure is therefore a debt the player took on when they made the promise, and the cost of revocation scales with it. The decision points bite in sequence. First, in what order to revoke, because revoking the cashback offer first triggers a surge of completion attempts on the reward before the player can reach it. Second, how to treat people who have commenced but not completed, which is genuinely unsettled and which the game presents honestly: the player may choose to honour partial performers (expensive, reduces reputational damage) or to stand on the strict s 8 requirement that the conditions be performed (cheap, invites litigation and a Reputation hit that raises the cost of the third promise). Third, the standing offer to government departments has a different shape entirely, because each indent is a separate acceptance creating a separate contract, so revocation only stops future indents and cannot touch those already placed. Round three delivers a mass claim event, and the failure mode is the player who revoked cheaply and now faces a hundred claimants who commenced performance in reliance on a promise that was still visible on a partner's website.
modules.win_loss: Win by closing all three promises with accrued liability inside the board's cap and Reputation above the floor. Lose instructively by revoking with less publicity than the original promise, which does not close the exposure at all.
modules.build_notes: Each promise is an object with publicityReach (integer), conditions (array), commencedCount, completedCount and revocationChannels. Revocation succeeds only if the sum of revocation channel reach is at least publicityReach. Partial performers are a separate cohort with a configurable policy so the unsettled doctrine is visible as a designer choice.

modules.title: Can someone accept an offer without knowing about it?
modules.doctrine: Communication and knowledge of the proposal; accidental performance versus performance in response to an offer.
modules.mechanic: the player performs the requested act with different levels of knowledge and then attempts to claim the reward.
modules.authority: Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt, (1913) ILR 35 All 489
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three finders present claims. One saw the notice and then searched, one searched and then saw the notice, one searched with a vague sense that a reward existed but cannot say where they heard it. The player ranks the claims and sees where the line falls.
modules.lab: makes the player the claimant, and the game is played backwards from the claim. The player performs the recovery over four days and, at each day, chooses actions that either establish or fail to establish knowledge: reading the notice at a location with a camera, forwarding it to a colleague with a timestamp, mentioning it in a message, or simply proceeding. Every knowledge-establishing action costs time, and time matters because a rival is also searching and only the first successful recovery earns anything at all. This is the central tension: the actions that make the claim provable are the same actions that slow the player down. Claude plays the reward-giver with a policy of resisting the claim on the knowledge point and, if that fails, on whether the act performed was the act requested. That second line forces a further decision on day three, when the player discovers the consignment in a slightly different condition than the notice contemplated, and must choose between delivering it as found (fast, but arguably not the requested act) or restoring it first (slow, but squarely within the conditions). Round four adds a rival claimant who did read the notice and who will litigate, so the player's evidence file is tested against a competing one rather than against nothing. The failure mode is the player who recovers first, brilliantly, and cannot prove they had ever heard of the reward.
modules.win_loss: Win by recovering first with a provable knowledge timestamp preceding the recovery. Lose instructively by winning the race and losing the claim, or by building an unimpeachable evidence file too slowly and finishing second.
modules.build_notes: Each actor holds a knowledgeTimestamp (nullable) and an evidenceStrength score. Claim resolves only if knowledgeTimestamp precedes performanceTimestamp and evidenceStrength clears a threshold. The race is a simple tick counter where evidence actions cost ticks. Flag the Lalman Shukla citation for verification in the appendix.

modules.title: Did the reply accept the offer or destroy it?
modules.doctrine: Absolute and unqualified acceptance, counter-offers, qualified acceptance and requests for information.
modules.mechanic: respond to successive messages without accidentally rejecting the bargain or creating a counter-offer.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: five replies are shown ('I accept if you include insurance', 'Would you consider including insurance?', 'I accept, and please confirm delivery date', 'I accept at four lakhs' where the offer was four and a half, 'I accept'). The player marks each as acceptance, counter-offer or mere inquiry, then sees which one killed the deal.
modules.lab: is a full negotiation played over eight exchanges. The player wants three concessions (price, insurance, delivery timing) but every message they send is parsed by the doctrine before it is parsed by the counterparty. A request for information leaves the offer alive; a qualified acceptance kills it and hands the counterparty the power to refuse; an acceptance ends the game with whatever terms are on the table. The player therefore has a real linguistic problem: how to press for a concession in a form that reads as inquiry rather than qualification, knowing that the distinction is one of substance and not of politeness. Pressure escalates because the Patience meter falls faster when the player sends inquiries that are transparently disguised counter-offers, and because the counterparty's reserve is hidden, so the player never knows how much room is left. Two decision points are especially sharp. Around exchange four the counterparty sends an improved offer with a deadline, and the player must decide whether to accept a good deal or risk one more inquiry with a deadline running. Around exchange six the counterparty sends a reply that is itself ambiguous between acceptance and counter-offer, and the player must decide whether to treat it as an acceptance and start performing (fast, but if wrong they have accepted a counter-offer on worse terms) or to seek clarification (safe, but consumes patience). The failure mode that teaches most is the player who wins every concession and discovers that their penultimate message was a counter-offer, so the deal they thought they had closed never existed.
modules.win_loss: Win by concluding a binding contract with at least two of the three concessions before the counterparty walks. Lose instructively by killing a live offer with a qualified acceptance and finding that the counterparty's fresh offer is worse than the one destroyed.
modules.build_notes: Each player message is classified by a parser into acceptance, counterOffer or inquiry, with the classification and reasons shown after the turn. Killing the offer sets offerAlive to false and swaps offeror and offeree roles. Patience decrements are weighted by classification, penalising disguised counter-offers.

modules.title: Can conduct amount to acceptance?
modules.doctrine: Acceptance through performance, receipt of consideration and express or implied promises.
modules.mechanic: choose actions rather than words in transport, restaurant, subscription and service scenarios and observe when liability arises.
modules.authority: Bhagwandas Goverdhandas Kedia v Girdharilal Parshottamdas, AIR 1966 SC 543
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player moves through three of the six transactions choosing actions, not words, and then sees the Acceptance Ledger fill. The reveal is that the player has entered two contracts and avoided one.
modules.lab: sets a goal that sounds impossible and is not: obtain the benefit of all six services while accepting the terms of only two. This forces the player to look at each transaction and find where the conduct-equals-acceptance link is weakest. Some links are unbreakable, because taking the ride simply is acceptance under s 8; those transactions must be paid for or skipped, and part of the learning is recognising which ones they are. Others are breakable, and the ways of breaking them are precise legal moves: rejecting the sample rather than consuming it, terminating the trial before the notified change takes effect, parking in a lot where the notice appeared after the barrier rather than before it. The second half introduces the mirror problem. The player becomes a service designer whose revenue depends on conduct amounting to acceptance, and Claude plays a sophisticated consumer running exactly the moves the player just used. The designer must decide where to place the terms, when to place them relative to the benefit, and whether to require an affirmative act (higher legal certainty, lower conversion) or to rely on continued use (higher conversion, weaker acceptance). This is where the game generates its 'aha': the player discovers that the doctrinal question of when conduct accepts is identical to the design question of where in a flow to put the terms, which sets up Modules 48 and 51 directly. Failure mode is the designer who relies on continued use for a materially onerous term and finds that Claude's consumer took the benefit and repudiated the term.
modules.win_loss: Win as consumer by taking at least four benefits while accepting at most two term-sets; win as designer by achieving revenue target with an Acceptance Certainty score above threshold. Lose instructively by consuming a benefit whose acceptance link was unbreakable while believing you had avoided it.
modules.build_notes: Each transaction is an object with benefitTiming, termsTiming, affirmativeActRequired and a resolver returning accepted or not with reasons. The designer half reuses the same objects with the parameters exposed as controls, so the two halves are literally the same model played from both ends.

modules.title: At what precise moment is acceptance complete?
modules.doctrine: Different completion points against proposer and acceptor; postal and instantaneous communications.
modules.mechanic: place letters, calls and messages on a timeline and identify the exact moment each party becomes bound.
modules.authority: Bhagwandas Goverdhandas Kedia v Girdharilal Parshottamdas, AIR 1966 SC 543
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: one acceptance is sent by post and the price moves between dispatch and delivery. The player identifies who is bound at each of three timestamps, and sees the window in which one party is bound and the other is not.
modules.lab: is a trading game across five deals in a volatile market. The player is a trader who both sends and receives acceptances, and the channel choice is theirs each time. The physics is the s 4 asymmetry: by posting an acceptance the player binds the proposer immediately while remaining free themselves until the letter arrives, which creates a genuinely valuable option if the price moves in that window. Telephone destroys that option entirely under Kedia, because the acceptance is complete only when heard. Email sits in genuinely contested territory, which the game presents as a risk band rather than a settled rule, and the player must price that uncertainty. Escalation comes from the counterparty, played by Claude with a policy of preferring instantaneous channels when the market is moving in the player's favour and slow channels when it is not, which teaches the player to read channel choice as information. Three decision points recur. Whether to accept by post to capture the asymmetry window, knowing that s 5 lets the player revoke the acceptance by a faster message reaching the proposer before the acceptance does, which is the sharpest move in the whole module. Whether to send proposals by channels that shorten the counterparty's window. And whether to insist contractually on a prescribed mode, which drags Module 12 into play. Failure mode is a trader who uses the postal asymmetry aggressively, is caught by a counterparty who revokes the proposal before the letter is posted, and learns that the same asymmetry cuts both ways.
modules.win_loss: Win by closing the five deals with net profit above target. Lose instructively by being bound at a price you would not have accepted, having misread which clock governed.
modules.build_notes: Each channel is an object with transmissionLag and knowledgeLag distributions. Binding status is computed independently for each party from those timestamps. Price is a seeded series. Email should carry an explicit uncertaintyBand that widens outcomes rather than resolving cleanly, and the debrief must say why.

modules.title: Can an offeror prescribe the method of acceptance, or declare silence to be acceptance?
modules.doctrine: Prescribed modes, reasonable modes, waiver of defective mode and the general insufficiency of silence.
modules.mechanic: accept through email, app, post, performance or silence and test whether the offeror can object.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three deviating acceptances arrive. The player chooses to object or stay silent on each and immediately sees which prescription survived and which was waived by inaction.
modules.lab: is a procurement season with twelve deviating acceptances arriving on a schedule, and here is the trap that makes it a strategy game: the player does not want to object to all of them. Some deviations are commercially convenient (a supplier who starts work immediately when the player is behind schedule), and objecting would delay delivery. But s 7(2) does not let the player pick and choose retroactively, because a pattern of silent acceptance across a relationship makes it progressively harder to insist on the prescribed mode later, and Claude, playing the supplier side, tracks that pattern and pleads it. So the decisions are about consistency under commercial pressure. Objecting always is legally clean and operationally expensive. Objecting selectively is cheap now and erodes the prescription. A third option, which the game rewards for players who find it, is to re-issue the prescription formally at the start of each order cycle, which resets the position without refusing any individual delivery. Round three introduces the silence variant: a supplier ships without any communication at all, and the player must decide whether to treat the shipment as acceptance under s 8 (binding, at the player's own prices) or to reject it, which involves storage and return costs and risks the season. Round four introduces a supplier who tries the reverse move, purporting to make the player's silence an acceptance of a price increase, which is the same doctrine used against the player and which the player must refuse correctly rather than merely ignore. Failure mode is the player who ignores the price-increase notice on the theory that silence is never acceptance and finds that their continued ordering constituted acceptance by conduct under s 8.
modules.win_loss: Win by completing the season on schedule with the prescription intact and no accepted price increase. Lose instructively by waiving the prescription through a pattern of silence, or by ignoring the price-increase notice while continuing to order.
modules.build_notes: Each acceptance object has prescribedMode, actualMode, communicatedAt and objectedAt (nullable). Waiver resolves if objectedAt is null past the reasonableWindow, or via a patternScore across the relationship. The price-increase event must be resolvable by three distinct player moves (explicit rejection, stopping orders, or objecting and continuing) with different outcomes.

modules.title: Who wins the revocation race?
modules.doctrine: Revocation of proposals and acceptances, communication requirements and different statutory deadlines.
modules.mechanic: dispatch competing letters, calls and instant messages before the legal window closes.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: one proposal, one acceptance in the post, and a revocation the player must decide how to send. The reveal shows that a revocation of proposal sent after posting arrives too late, while a revocation of acceptance sent by telegram can still overtake the letter.
modules.lab: runs four simultaneous transactions in a market that moves each turn, and the player is proposer in two and acceptor in two. The core engine is that the two windows close at different moments, so at any given tick the player may be free in one deal and locked in another, and the price movement makes some escapes valuable and others pointless. Each turn the player has a limited number of message slots, so they cannot revoke everything they would like to; they must triage. Three decisions carry the game. Channel selection at the time of proposing, because proposing by post gives the player a long window to revoke but also gives the acceptor a long window to post an acceptance that binds the player before they know of it. Whether to spend a scarce fast-channel slot overtaking one's own posted acceptance, which is the s 5 move that most students never see used, and which is only worth doing when the price has moved enough to justify burning the slot. And whether to deliberately delay reading incoming messages, which sounds clever until the player discovers that communication of a proposal is complete on knowledge, so refusing to read a revocation of proposal may keep the proposal alive for the player's benefit, while refusing to read an acceptance does not help them at all because they were bound the moment it was posted. Round four adds a counterparty who dies mid-transaction, pulling s 6 into the race, so the player must recompute every window. Failure mode is a player who wins three races and loses the fourth for want of a message slot, which teaches triage as a legal skill.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending the four transactions with net position above target. Lose instructively by sending a technically correct revocation that arrives one tick late, which is the whole point of the module.
modules.build_notes: Model messages as objects in transit with dispatchTick and arrivalTick. Compute proposerWindowOpen and acceptorWindowOpen independently each tick from ss 4 and 5. Message slots are a per-turn resource. Section 6 lapse events (death, insanity, time) fire on a schedule and must recompute all windows.

modules.title: Must a contract be written, signed or registered?
modules.anchor: ICA s 10 saving clause; IT Act ss 4, 5, 10A; transaction-specific statutes
modules.doctrine: General contractual informality versus statutory requirements of writing, signature, stamping or registration.
modules.mechanic: route transactions through oral, written, electronic, signed and registered pathways without adding unnecessary formalities.
modules.authority: Trimex International FZE Ltd v Vedanta Aluminium Ltd, (2010) 3 SCC 1
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three transactions are routed by the player and the results shown. The intended surprise is that the cheapest valid route for a common commercial supply agreement is far less formal than most learners expect, while one apparently minor transaction turns out to require registration.
modules.lab: gives the player a startup's entire first-year contracting programme with a fixed legal budget and a launch deadline. Eight transactions must be routed: a founders' arrangement, a lease, an employment agreement, a supply contract, a customer terms-of-service, an assignment of a receivable, a family loan funding the venture, and a transfer of immovable property. The physics is that formality is a cost with a discontinuous benefit: below the mandatory threshold the transaction is void or unenforceable no matter how well documented, and above it the extra formality buys only evidentiary comfort. The strategic tension is budget against risk under a deadline, and it is sharpened by two mechanics. First, a Challenge event in round three tests three randomly chosen transactions, and under-formalised ones fail while over-formalised ones survive but have already consumed budget that the player now needs elsewhere. Second, the electronic pathway is cheap and fast under IT Act ss 4, 5 and 10A but carries a carve-out the player must find: certain instruments are excluded from electronic execution, and routing an excluded instrument electronically produces a confident-looking document with no legal effect, which is the most instructive failure in the game. Round four adds a funding due diligence in which every under-documented transaction becomes a discount on valuation, so evidentiary formality that seemed wasteful acquires a price.
modules.win_loss: Win by launching on time with all eight transactions surviving the Challenge and the due diligence discount below threshold. Lose instructively by routing an excluded instrument through the electronic pathway, or by spending the budget on notarising a contract that never needed it and having nothing left for the registrable one.
modules.build_notes: Each transaction type carries mandatoryFormality (enum), electronicEligible (boolean), and evidentiaryCurve. Route selection below mandatory level sets enforceable to false regardless of other attributes. The Challenge event samples transactions and applies the enforceability check. Keep the electronic exclusion list as configurable data, since it is statute-specific and will change.

modules.title: When does an offer die without express revocation?
modules.doctrine: Rejection, lapse of prescribed or reasonable time, failure of condition precedent, death and insanity.
modules.mechanic: maintain or terminate several offers while time and external events advance.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four offers are shown at different ages and the player predicts which are still alive. The reveal makes the point that reasonable time is not a fixed number but a function of the subject matter, so a perishable-goods offer dies far faster than a land offer of the same age.
modules.lab: runs twelve weeks. Prices move, so the value of each offer changes, and the player has a limited number of actions per week. Available actions are: accept (converting the offer into a contract and removing it from the portfolio), seek an extension (which requires the proposer's assent and may prompt them to withdraw), fulfil a condition precedent (costly, and wasted if the player later declines), or do nothing. The physics is that doing nothing is not free: reasonable time keeps running, and the offers that are most valuable are usually the ones most likely to be revoked by a proposer watching the same price movement. The sharpest mechanic is the knowledge requirement in the death and insanity limb. Two proposers in the portfolio are at risk, and the offer only dies if the fact comes to the acceptor's knowledge before acceptance. This creates an uncomfortable and highly instructive decision: the player may become aware that a proposer is gravely ill and must decide whether to accept quickly, and whether to open the message that would give them the knowledge that kills the offer. The game does not moralise about this, it just resolves it under s 6, and the debrief raises the ethical dimension explicitly rather than pretending the incentive does not exist. Round three introduces a condition precedent that costs a third of the portfolio's action budget, forcing the player to commit before knowing whether prices will justify it. Failure mode is a player who holds every offer open, hedging, and finds in week ten that the three valuable ones lapsed while they were extending the worthless ones.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending week twelve with accepted contracts above the value target. Lose instructively by letting a high-value offer die on reasonable time while nursing offers whose conditions could never be met.
modules.build_notes: Each offer object holds prescribedTime (nullable), subjectMatterVolatility, conditionPrecedent (nullable), proposerRiskFlag and a computed reasonableTime derived from volatility. Death or insanity kills an offer only when knowledgeFlag is set on the acceptor, and the knowledge event must be a player-visible choice to open a message.

modules.title: Did the negotiations ever become a completed agreement?
modules.doctrine: "Subject to contract," heads of terms, agreements to agree, unresolved essential matters and incomplete bargains.
modules.mechanic: inspect successive drafts and decide at which version, if any, the negotiations became binding.
modules.authority: Kollipara Sriramulu v T Aswatha Narayana, AIR 1968 SC 1028
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player reads five successive versions of a term sheet and marks the version, if any, at which a binding agreement arose. The reveal shows that the label on the document mattered less than a delivery that occurred between versions three and four.
modules.lab: plays the negotiation forward across ten drafting turns. The player is one side, Claude the other, and each turn each side can settle a term, insert or remove 'subject to contract' language, propose a mechanism for an unsettled term, or perform an act (advance a payment, begin mobilisation, take delivery of a sample). The physics runs on two axes at once. Certainty under s 29 rises as terms are settled or as objective mechanisms are supplied, so a price 'to be agreed' is fatal while a price 'as determined by a named valuer' is not. Bindingness rises with conduct and falls with express reservations, and it is computed separately for each party, which is where the asymmetry lives. The decisions are genuinely two-sided. Supplying a valuation mechanism cures the s 29 defect but also removes the player's ability to walk away over price, so a player who wants optionality must keep something uncertain, and yet keeping too much uncertain means there is no deal to enforce if the counterparty walks. Inserting 'subject to contract' protects the player but Claude will mirror it, and mutual reservations mean neither side is bound while both are spending. Around turn seven Claude begins performing, which is the crucial pressure: performance raises the player's bindingness whether or not they wanted it, and the player must decide whether to accept the benefit (binding, but the deal advances) or refuse it (unbound, but the counterparty may walk). The failure mode is the player who reserves perfectly, is never bound, and watches the counterparty walk away in turn nine having spent nine turns of the player's own resources.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending with the counterparty bound on terms certain enough to survive s 29 while your own exposure is limited to the terms you chose. Lose instructively either by being bound first, or by preserving perfect optionality until the deal evaporates.
modules.build_notes: Maintain a term matrix with status settled, mechanism or open. Certainty resolves per s 29 from that matrix. Bindingness is per-party, incremented by conduct and decremented by express reservation, and both values must be visible to the player at all times. Claude's policy: mirror reservations, begin performing at turn seven, walk at turn nine if not bound.

modules.title: What can count as consideration?
modules.doctrine: An act, abstinence or promise undertaken at the promisor's desire.
modules.mechanic: connect promises and performances with arrows until each legally supports the other.
modules.authority: Durga Prasad v Baldeo, (1880) ILR 3 All 221
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three acts are shown, each benefiting the same promisor. One was requested specifically, one was requested vaguely by someone else, one was purely voluntary. The player identifies which supports a promise to pay, and sees that benefit alone is legally inert.
modules.lab: puts the player in the position of someone who has already acted and now wants payment, which is the hard direction. They have built an access road that benefits the shopkeepers and increased everyone's takings, but no one asked for it in terms. The player has six moves and a shrinking window before memories and records harden, and each move is an attempt to establish a desire link retrospectively without fabricating anything: obtaining a written acknowledgment that the work was done at the collector's suggestion, finding the meeting minute that records a request, getting a shopkeeper to request the second phase (which converts phase two into good consideration but does nothing for phase one), or reframing the claim under s 70 as a lawful non-gratuitous act, which is a different cause of action with different requirements. Claude plays the shopkeepers with a policy of conceding benefit freely (it is obvious and undeniable) while denying any request, which forces the player to notice that benefit and desire are separate elements and that the opponent will happily give away the one that does not matter. The sharpest decision is around move four, when the player can secure a fresh promise to pay from one shopkeeper in exchange for a future abstention, which is clean consideration under s 2(d) and covers only that shopkeeper, versus spending the same move chasing the collective claim that would cover everyone but may fail entirely. Round three introduces a rival who did the work under an express request and is paid immediately, which makes the structural lesson visceral. Failure mode is a player who accumulates overwhelming evidence of benefit and loses on the desire link.
modules.win_loss: Win by establishing an enforceable claim over at least half the value, whether through the desire link or by correctly pivoting to s 70. Lose instructively by proving benefit exhaustively while the desire link stays empty.
modules.build_notes: Each act object holds requestedBy (nullable), requestSpecificity (0 to 3), beneficiary and actorId. Consideration resolves only where requestedBy equals promisorId and specificity is at least 1. Benefit is a separate visible attribute deliberately disconnected from the resolver, so the player can see it doing nothing.

modules.title: Whose act can provide consideration?
modules.doctrine: Indian law permits consideration to move from the promisee or another person, but the act must be at the promisor's desire.
modules.mechanic: allocate benefits and performances among promisor, promisee and a third person.
modules.authority: Chinnaya v Ramaya, (1882) ILR 4 Mad 137
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a family arrangement in which a mother transfers property to her son on his promise to pay an annuity to her sister. The player marks whether the promise is supported by consideration and, separately, who can enforce it. The reveal is that the answers come apart.
modules.lab: is a structuring exercise. The player is advising on a supply chain financing arrangement where a buyer wants a supplier's obligation guaranteed but the supplier's parent will not sign, and the money that would support the promise sits in a third entity. The player must build a structure in which every promise is supported by consideration under s 2(d), using the Indian latitude on who supplies it, while keeping the person who will need to sue in a position to do so. Six structural moves are available, each with a cost and a tax or commercial side-effect, and the board recomputes both lights after every move. The tension is that the moves which most easily supply consideration from a third party are the moves that most weaken the enforcing party's standing, because routing value through a third entity tends to leave the intended claimant outside the promise. The player must therefore learn to separate two questions that look like one. Round two adds a stress: one of the third parties withdraws, and the player must rebuild consideration for two promises with one move. Round three tests the structure by having Claude, as counsel for the promisor, attack it, using a policy of first denying the promisor's desire (Module 17's element, which the Indian latitude does not relax) and then arguing that the intended claimant is a stranger to the contract. Failure mode is an elegant structure in which every promise is supported and nobody who cares about performance can sue.
modules.win_loss: Win by producing a structure where all promises are supported and the intended enforcer has standing, within the cost budget. Lose instructively by building a fully supported structure with no enforceable route, which is the single most common error the Indian rule invites.
modules.build_notes: Represent the deal as a directed graph with nodes for parties and edges typed as promise, act, payment or request. Two independent resolvers: considerationExists(edge) and hasStanding(party, edge). Render them as separate indicators, never combined. The English-rule toggle changes one condition in the first resolver only.

modules.title: Can an earlier act support a later promise?
modules.doctrine: Past, executed and executory consideration; requested past performance versus voluntary action.
modules.mechanic: rearrange request, performance and promise cards to determine whether consideration exists.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four transactions with different orderings. The player identifies which are supported, and the reveal contrasts the Indian position with the English one so the learner does not import the wrong rule from textbooks.
modules.lab: is a drafting and advisory game across a professional services relationship. The player is a consultant who has done a great deal of work in a fluid arrangement where requests were informal, some work was volunteered to impress the client, and a promise to pay a lump sum came only at the end. The client, played by Claude, now disputes the lump sum with a policy of admitting the work, admitting the promise, and denying that any of it was requested, which is precisely the attack that makes past consideration fail. The player has eight investigation and drafting moves. Investigation moves surface evidence about whether particular tranches of work were requested, and the discovery is granular: some tranches were requested and some were not, so the claim splits. Drafting moves let the player restructure what remains, and the key strategic choice arrives here. For requested past work, s 2(d) supplies consideration and the lump sum promise is enforceable. For volunteered work, s 2(d) is closed, and the player must either obtain a written and registered promise under s 25(1) (expensive, requires the client's cooperation, which Claude will resist) or bring the promise within s 25(2) as compensation for something the promisor was legally compellable to do or which was done voluntarily for the promisor, whose elements are narrower than most learners assume and which the game enforces strictly. A third route, quantum meruit under s 70, is available but yields a different measure and forfeits the agreed lump sum, so choosing it is a real trade-off rather than a fallback. Failure mode is a player who litigates the whole lump sum on one theory and loses the requested tranches along with the volunteered ones.
modules.win_loss: Win by recovering the maximum aggregate across correctly chosen routes. Lose instructively by insisting on a single theory for a factually mixed claim.
modules.build_notes: Each work tranche is an object with requestedFlag, performedAt, promisedAt and value. Route availability is computed per tranche by a rules table (s 2(d), s 25(1), s 25(2), s 70) with the failing element named. The UI must allow the player to assign different tranches to different routes and to see the aggregate.

modules.title: Is consideration always necessary?
modules.doctrine: Consideration as the general price of enforceability; distinguishing consideration from motive, affection and gifts.
modules.mechanic: each promise must pass through consideration or a recognized statutory exception.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four promises approach the gate (a promise to a brother out of affection, unregistered; a promise to pay a time-barred debt, oral; a promise to pay for work already done at request; a promise of a gift already delivered). The player sends each to a lane and sees which pass.
modules.lab: makes the player a family office lawyer with eight promises to make enforceable before a succession event, a fixed budget, and a registration office that takes days. The physics is that s 25's exceptions are conjunctive: near relation and natural love and affection and writing and registration must all be present, and the game refuses to let a strong showing on one element compensate for a missing other, which is exactly how the section operates and exactly the intuition learners bring and lose on. The strategic layer is resource allocation under a deadline. Registration is the scarcest resource, so the player must decide which promises truly need the s 25(1) route and which can be converted into ordinary consideration-supported bargains by adding a small reciprocal obligation, which is cheaper and faster but changes the character of the transaction and may have tax and family consequences the game surfaces. The time-barred debt promise under s 25(3) needs only writing and signature, so it is cheap, but the player must first determine whether the debt is in fact barred, and the game includes one debt that is not barred, where the s 25(3) route is unnecessary and the promise is unsupported for a different reason. Round three introduces a challenge from a disappointed relative, played by Claude, who attacks the weakest latch on each promise. The failure mode that teaches most is the player who registers a promise between parties who are not in a near relation, spending the scarcest resource on a lane that was never open.
modules.win_loss: Win by having at least six of eight promises enforceable at the succession event within budget. Lose instructively by satisfying three of four elements on several promises, which yields nothing at all.
modules.build_notes: Each s 25 sub-clause is a conjunctive latch set. The gate resolver must report the specific missing latch, never a generic failure. Registration is a queued resource with a day cost. Include at least one trap promise where the chosen exception was never applicable.

modules.title: Which promises survive without consideration?
modules.doctrine: Registered promises based on natural love and affection, compensation for voluntary acts, written promises to pay time-barred debts and completed gifts.
modules.mechanic: collect every statutory element needed to unlock enforceability for each no-consideration promise.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player takes one promise to each door and discovers that the s 25(1) door needs four elements while the s 25(3) door needs two, and that one promise in the set does not need a door at all.
modules.lab: is an estate-and-obligations puzzle across three months. The player holds nine promises and a limited stock of elements: two registrations, four notarised writings, a finite number of counterparty signatures (each requiring persuasion, because the promisors have their own interests), and a legal opinion budget for determining which debts are actually time-barred. The scarce resources force genuine prioritisation. The design keeps three decision points live. First, near relation and natural love and affection are not the same element, and the game includes a pair who are near relations but between whom the surrounding facts negative affection, which is a real line in the decided cases and which the player must detect from the file rather than assume from the relationship. Second, s 25(2) rewards precision about who the voluntary act was done for: an act done for a family generally does not support a promise by one member, and the player must either find the specific beneficiary or abandon the route. Third, the completed gift door is quietly the best answer for two of the nine, and the player who notices this frees registrations for promises that genuinely need them. Claude plays a disappointed heir who challenges each enforceable promise at the end, attacking the element with the thinnest evidence. Failure mode is a player who treats near relation as sufficient for s 25(1) and finds two registrations spent on promises that fail on affection.
modules.win_loss: Win by making at least seven of nine promises effective, counting completed gifts. Lose instructively by exhausting registrations on the s 25(1) door for promises that could have been completed as gifts.
modules.build_notes: Elements are inventory items consumed on use. Each door is a conjunctive checker naming the missing element. Include an affirmative negation of affection in one file so the check is evidentiary, not relational. The gift door should require a completion action (delivery or transfer) rather than a promise object.

modules.title: Must consideration be economically adequate?
modules.doctrine: Inadequacy does not itself invalidate a bargain, but may evidence lack of free consent; consideration must nevertheless be real.
modules.mechanic: negotiate at highly unequal prices while hidden facts test whether the issue is inadequacy or impaired consent.
modules.authority: Chidambara Iyer v P S Renga Iyer, AIR 1966 SC 193
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player sees a sale at a quarter of market value and must say whether it is void. The reveal is that it is not, and then two facts are added from Tray B and the picture changes, which shows precisely what inadequacy does and does not do.
modules.lab: is played twice, once from each side, which is what makes the doctrine land. In the first half the player acts for the seller seeking to set aside the sale. Inadequacy is on the record already and is worth nothing on its own, so every move must convert the price gap into evidence about the seller's consent: establishing the buyer's position of dominance under s 16, showing the absence of independent advice, showing the seller's distress at the time. The player has seven investigative moves and Claude, for the buyer, responds by populating Tray A, offering innocent explanations for the price that are individually plausible. In the second half the player switches sides and defends an equally cheap purchase, now with the burden question live. The physics here connects directly to Module 32: once the transaction appears unconscionable and a dominating relationship is shown, s 16(3) shifts the burden onto the person in the dominant position, so the defence's real objective is not to explain the price but to prevent the burden from shifting in the first place. That reframing is the payoff. The sharpest decision arrives when the player, as defender, can produce evidence of the seller's independent legal advice, which is powerful but also confirms that the buyer knew the price was low enough to need advice, and Claude will use that admission. Failure mode in the first half is a player who proves the price gap magnificently and never touches consent; failure mode in the second is a player who explains the price so thoroughly that they establish their own awareness of the seller's vulnerability.
modules.win_loss: Win in each half by moving the Consent Doubt meter past or below the threshold within the move budget. Lose instructively by treating inadequacy as a ground rather than as evidence, which produces a strong-looking case that does nothing.
modules.build_notes: Validity must be hard-coded to ignore priceRatio entirely; only consentDoubt responds to it, and then only in combination with at least one relationship or vulnerability fact. Expose this in the debrief as a rule the player can read. Burden shifting should be a visible state change carried over into Module 32.

modules.title: Can a creditor accept less or waive part of performance without fresh consideration?
modules.doctrine: Remission, extension of time, waiver and acceptance of another satisfaction; distinction from novation.
modules.mechanic: negotiate among immediate part-payment, delayed full payment and alternative satisfaction while managing enforcement risk.
modules.authority: Kapurchand Godha v Mir Nawab Himayat Ali Khan Azamjah, AIR 1963 SC 250
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a debtor offers sixty per cent in full and final settlement. The player accepts or refuses, and the reveal shows that under s 63 acceptance discharges the balance without fresh consideration, which surprises anyone taught the English rule first.
modules.lab: runs a workout across four quarters. The player is the creditor with a recovery target, five debtors, and limited enforcement capacity so they cannot pursue everyone. The engine is that every concession is legally effective at once. An extension of time under s 63 is binding, so it cannot be withdrawn when the market turns; a remission of part is a discharge of that part, so it cannot be revived when the debtor's fortunes improve, which happens to one debtor in quarter three and is the game's cruellest and most instructive moment. Three strategic problems run in parallel. First, sequencing: conceding to the weakest debtor first is humane and sets a precedent the other four will invoke, and Claude, playing the debtors collectively, does invoke it. Second, the limitation clock, which interacts with concessions in ways the player must think about, because an extension granted casually can leave the creditor with a debt that has become difficult to enforce, and the s 25(3) route in Module 21 then becomes the only repair. Third, the boundary with s 62: accepting a substituted obligation from a third party or on materially different terms may be a novation that discharges the original contract entirely, including securities, rather than a remission of part, and the player must decide in quarter two whether to accept a restructured obligation from a debtor's group company, which improves the covenant and may silently release the security. Failure mode is a creditor who extends generously in quarter one, discovers in quarter three that the improved debtor cannot be pursued for the remitted portion, and has no security left on the restructured one.
modules.win_loss: Win by hitting the recovery target across four quarters with securities intact. Lose instructively by remitting portions of debts that later became fully recoverable, or by converting a remission into an unintended novation.
modules.build_notes: Every player utterance to a debtor must be classified by a resolver into remission, extension, satisfaction, novation or no concession, and logged irreversibly. Novation must trigger a security-release check. Limitation is a per-debt clock affected by extensions and acknowledgments.

modules.title: Can a minor enter a contract?
modules.doctrine: Majority as a condition of competency; the voidness of a minor's agreement is principally developed through Indian case law.
modules.mechanic: determine contractual capacity across birthdays, misstatements of age and transactions made through adults.
modules.authority: Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, (1903) 30 IA 114
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player lends against security to someone who signs a declaration of majority, and then discovers the borrower was seventeen. The reveal is that the declaration is worth nothing, and that estoppel does not rescue the lender where the lender's agent knew or could have known.
modules.lab: is a full underwriting cycle with a portfolio target and a verification budget. Verification is costly and slows deals, and competitors will take any business the player refuses, so refusing to lend to anyone who looks young is not a viable strategy. The player must therefore allocate verification spend by risk, and the game rewards reading the transaction rather than the person: a small sale of goods to a young buyer is a different exposure from a mortgage. Three mechanics create the depth. First, the player can take security, guarantees or a parent's co-signature, and the game distinguishes sharply between these: security given by the minor is worthless because the underlying agreement is void, while an independent obligation from a competent adult is not, and learning that distinction is the module's commercial core. Second, the misrepresentation route is closed, and Claude, playing the minor's guardian, will plead minority even where the minor lied, so the player who relies on the declaration loses. Third, a partial escape exists but only for necessaries under s 68, which points forward to Module 27 and applies to the minor's property rather than to the minor personally, so it works for some transactions in the book and not others. Round four brings a portfolio review where every void transaction is written off, and the player sees which underwriting decisions actually protected them.
modules.win_loss: Win by hitting the portfolio target with write-offs below threshold. Lose instructively by relying on a declaration of age, on security given by the minor, or on the assumption that a lie shifts the risk.
modules.build_notes: Minor counterparties must have enforceable set permanently false, unaffected by declarations, security or estoppel flags, and the resolver must say so explicitly. Adult co-obligor objects are separate contracts with their own resolvers. Necessaries claims resolve against the minor's property pool only.

modules.title: Can a defective minor's transaction be ratified or unwound later?
modules.anchor: ICA ss 11, 65; SRA s 33; case law
modules.doctrine: Ratification after majority, estoppel, restitution and protection against indirectly enforcing a void agreement.
modules.mechanic: make decisions before and after the player turns eighteen and track which obligations can legally survive.
modules.authority: Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, (1903) 30 IA 114
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a loan taken at seventeen, followed at nineteen by a written confirmation promising to repay. The player predicts whether the confirmation works. The reveal is that ratification of a void agreement is not possible and the confirmation lacks fresh consideration, so the promise fails on both limbs.
modules.lab: gives the player the creditor's position across a five-year timeline with four transactions straddling the majority line, and a set of moves available at chosen points on the timeline. The physics is strict: nothing done after majority can breathe life into the earlier agreement, so the only productive post-majority move is to create a genuinely new contract with genuinely new consideration, and the game tests that consideration hard, rejecting a bare acknowledgment or a promise 'in consideration of the earlier loan'. The richest decisions arise around the restitution route. If the former minor sues to recover property transferred under the void transaction, SRA s 33 puts restoration in play, so the creditor's strategy may be to provoke or await a claim rather than to sue, which is a genuinely counter-intuitive posture and the game rewards a player who finds it. Against that, waiting has costs: the property may be dissipated, and limitation runs. Claude plays the former minor with a policy of avoiding court entirely once advised, which means the player cannot rely on the s 33 route arriving on its own. Round three introduces a fresh advance made after majority secured on the same property, which is the practical repair used in real lending, and the player must decide whether to make it at a moment when the borrower's position has weakened. Failure mode is a creditor who takes a beautifully drafted post-majority acknowledgment and holds an unenforceable document.
modules.win_loss: Win by recovering value through a fresh contract or through restitution when the former minor seeks relief. Lose instructively by relying on ratification, which is the error the module exists to kill.
modules.build_notes: Hard-block any state transition from void to valid triggered by post-majority acts. Fresh contracts must instantiate a new object with an independently validated consideration field. Section 33 restoration should activate only on a claim initiated by the former minor, so the player learns the procedural asymmetry.

modules.title: Was the person of sound mind at the moment of contracting?
modules.doctrine: Functional and transaction-specific understanding, rational judgment, lucid intervals and temporary incapacity.
modules.mechanic: review medical, behavioural and transaction evidence at different times before approving or rejecting the contract.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a will-adjacent transaction signed at 4 pm. The player is shown a diagnosis from six months earlier and asked whether the contract stands. The reveal is that a general condition does not decide it, and that the two evidence tokens nearest the execution moment do most of the work.
modules.lab: runs the module twice from opposite chairs and is unusually careful in tone, because the subject touches real vulnerability and the design must not encourage predatory framing. In the first half the player is the solicitor arranging the transaction and wants it to be unimpeachable later. Their moves are all about creating contemporaneous evidence at the execution moment: timing the signing for a period of best functioning, matching the explanation to the complexity of the transaction (a simple sale needs less understanding than a leveraged one, which the game models directly by scaling the required Understanding score to the transaction's complexity), obtaining a same-day assessment, recording the person explaining the transaction back in their own words. Every move costs time and some risk giving offence, and the counterparty is impatient. In the second half the player challenges a different transaction on behalf of a family member, and the physics is the same evidence model seen from the other side. The decisive discovery is that the strongest challenge is not medical but transactional: showing that the person could not have understood this particular arrangement's effect on their interests, which is why the complexity rating matters more than the diagnosis. Claude defends with a policy of pointing to lucid conduct elsewhere on the same day. The sharpest decision is whether to challenge at all, because a failed challenge is costly and the family relationship is a modelled resource. Failure mode in the first half is a solicitor who gathers excellent general medical evidence and nothing from the execution hour; in the second, a challenger who leads with the diagnosis and is defeated by a video of a coherent signing.
modules.win_loss: Win by producing (or defeating) a transaction whose capacity record holds at the execution moment for a transaction of that complexity. Lose instructively by arguing status rather than moment.
modules.build_notes: requiredUnderstanding must be a function of transactionComplexity. Evidence tokens carry a timestamp and a decay function so distance from the execution moment reduces weight. Keep the framing supportive: the interface should present the person as a rights-holder, and the debrief should address the ethics of capacity assessment directly.

modules.title: Who pays for necessaries supplied to an incapable person?
modules.doctrine: Reimbursement from the incapable person's property, meaning of "necessaries," suitability to condition in life and absence of personal contractual liability.
modules.mechanic: purchase food, education, luxury goods and medical services for an incapable person and identify recoverable expenditure.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the same item, a laptop, is supplied to all three. The player predicts recoverability in each case, and the reveal is that the answer differs by condition in life and by what the person already has, which is the relative standard in operation.
modules.lab: runs a supplier's business over three months with a working capital constraint and competitors. The player receives orders and must decide which to fulfil. The physics has three teeth. First, suitability is relative, so an item recoverable for one customer is not recoverable for another. Second, an item ceases to be a necessary if the person is already adequately supplied, which means the supplier must know what the customer already has, and acquiring that knowledge costs a move and may cost the sale. Third, recovery runs against the property pool only, so a customer with no property produces no recovery however necessary the goods were, which is uncomfortable and is exactly what the section says. The strategic decisions therefore sit at intake rather than at litigation. Should the supplier ask about existing provision (protects recoverability, loses sales to a competitor who does not ask)? Should the supplier extend to the wealthy minor items that would be luxuries for the poor one (recoverable here, and the game requires the player to justify by condition in life rather than by price)? Should the supplier serve the adult of unsound mind at all, given that his property pool is being consumed by earlier suppliers, which introduces a queue problem the player can only see by investigating? Month three adds an emergency medical supply to a person with almost no property, where the legally correct answer and the humane one diverge, and the game makes the player choose without pretending the law resolves it. Failure mode is a supplier who fulfils every order and discovers that half the book was luxuries and a quarter had no property behind it.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending three months solvent with recoverable claims above target. Lose instructively by supplying goods that were necessaries in the abstract but not suited to this person's condition in life, or by supplying against an exhausted property pool.
modules.build_notes: Necessity resolves from a function of (itemCategory, conditionInLife, existingProvision). Recovery amount is capped by propertyPool and reduced by prior claims, so a queue exists. Never allow personal liability. Handle the month-three dilemma without a scored 'right' answer; debrief it as a limit of the section.

modules.title: Did the parties agree upon the same thing in the same sense?
modules.doctrine: Consensus ad idem; different understandings of subject matter, quantity, identity or terms.
modules.mechanic: each party sees a different transaction description; the learner compares their mental models.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a sale of 'the consignment in the Kandla warehouse' where two consignments are there. The player asks one clarifying question of their choice and sees whether it lands on the divergent element. The reveal separates s 13 (no consent) from s 20 (shared mistake) explicitly, because learners routinely merge them.
modules.lab: runs a cross-border commodity sale over eight turns with six deal elements (identity of goods, quantity basis, quality standard, delivery point, currency, and the meaning of a trade term). Two elements are divergent from the start and the player does not know which. Each turn the player can ask one clarifying question, perform one act of performance, or send one confirmation. Questions reveal; performance advances the deal and raises Cost-to-Fix; confirmations lock an element as understood, which is powerful because a locked element that later proves divergent becomes the counterparty's problem rather than the player's. The genuine tension is that clarifying questions signal doubt, and Claude's counterparty is a trader whose policy is to re-price whenever the player reveals uncertainty about an element on which the counterparty holds the better information. So the player pays commercially for every question, and must guess which elements are worth interrogating. Turn five delivers a shipment discrepancy, and the player must decide their theory: pleading no consent under s 13 wipes the transaction and returns both sides to square one, which is good if the market has moved against the player and terrible if they need the goods; alternatively, treating the contract as formed and suing on the term is available only if the divergence is characterised as a term dispute rather than an absence of agreement. Choosing a theory forecloses the other, and the game makes the player choose before the market fully resolves. Failure mode is a player who confirms everything early to look decisive and locks in the counterparty's meaning on the one element that mattered.
modules.win_loss: Win by closing the transaction with no unresolved divergence on a value-critical element, or by selecting the theory that fits the post-discrepancy market. Lose instructively by discovering both divergences after delivery, when Cost-to-Fix exceeds the deal margin.
modules.build_notes: Maintain two independent meaning objects per element and never let the interface show the counterparty's value except through a question action. Theory selection at turn five should hard-branch the endgame and produce different restitution flows, so the strategic consequence is felt rather than described.

modules.title: Was consent free, and did the defect cause the agreement?
modules.doctrine: Taxonomy of coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation and mistake; causation and voidability.
modules.mechanic: trace the learner's decision through a causal map and identify the legally operative influence.
