modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four influences are presented and the player picks which one to run. The reveal shows that the best-evidenced influence (a false statement in a brochure) was not what moved the client, whereas the poorly-evidenced one (the adviser's pressure) was.
modules.lab: is an eight-move investigation and pleading exercise. The player must reconstruct why their client signed, using witness moves, document moves and client interview moves, each of which can strengthen either an element or a causal edge but not both. That forced choice is the heart of the design: with a fixed budget the player cannot fully prove any factor and must decide where to be strong. A factor with a perfect element score and a weak causal edge fails under s 19; so does the reverse. Two further mechanics generate depth. First, the proviso to s 19: if the player runs misrepresentation, Claude will plead that the client had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, and the player must have spent moves establishing why ordinary diligence would not have revealed it, which is a cost they had to incur before knowing the defence would be run. Notably that proviso does not touch coercion or undue influence, so a player who anticipates it may prefer a harder-to-prove factor with no diligence defence. Second, factors interact: undue influence and misrepresentation pleaded together can undercut each other, because a client dominated to the point of not exercising judgment is a client who was not relying on the representation. Claude exploits inconsistent pleading directly. Round three forces an election, and the failure mode is a player who pleads everything, proves several elements, and cannot show that any single one caused the signature.
modules.win_loss: Win by carrying one factor across both the element and causation thresholds. Lose instructively by spreading the budget across four factors, or by choosing a factor exposed to the s 19 proviso without having pre-funded the diligence answer.
modules.build_notes: Element and causation must be separate score fields per factor, with independent thresholds, and the interface must never merge them. Pleading multiple factors should apply an inconsistency penalty computed from a defined incompatibility matrix, shown to the player in the debrief.

modules.title: Was the pressure legally coercive?
modules.doctrine: Threatened prohibited acts, unlawful detention of property, territorial irrelevance and restitution of coerced payments.
modules.mechanic: decide whether to pay, resist or rescind while property and deadlines are used as pressure.
modules.authority: Chikkam Ammiraju v Chikkam Seshamma, (1917) ILR 41 Mad 33
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three pressure scenarios are shown (a threat to sue, a threat to report a genuine tax irregularity, a refusal to release goods over which the counterparty has no lien). The player marks which is coercion under s 15, and the reveal is that the intuitive ranking of nastiness does not match the legal one.
modules.lab: runs a six-day standoff with a clock. Demurrage bleeds the player daily, a downstream customer has a hard deadline, and the counterparty escalates its demands. The physics is precise. If the detention is lawful (a valid lien for unpaid charges), then the pressure is lawful and no amount of hardship converts it into coercion, so the player's money is gone once paid. If the detention is unlawful, then any payment extracted is recoverable under s 72 and the agreement is voidable under s 19, but only if the player can later prove the payment was made under that pressure rather than voluntarily, which is what the Protest Record is for. The decisions are all about acting under time pressure without destroying the later claim. Should the player pay now and preserve the downstream contract, and if so, in what terms? Paying with an unqualified settlement letter is fast and may extinguish the claim; paying under express protest preserves it but may provoke the counterparty into further delay, which Claude's policy does. Should the player seek urgent relief instead, which is slow and expensive but attacks the detention directly? Should the player investigate whether a lien exists at all, spending a day to find out, when that day may cost the downstream contract? Day four introduces a threat of a different kind, an accusation the counterparty says it will make to the authorities, and the player must classify it: a threat to do what one is lawfully entitled to do is not within s 15, while a threat to commit an offence is, and the difference is not about how frightening it is. Failure mode is a player who pays under crushing and entirely lawful pressure and then discovers there is nothing to recover.
modules.win_loss: Win by releasing the consignment in time with either the payment avoided or a live s 72 claim on a good Protest Record. Lose instructively by settling unconditionally, or by treating lawful commercial pressure as coercion and losing days to a hopeless position.
modules.build_notes: detentionLawful is a hidden boolean discoverable by an investigation action. Section 72 recoverability requires detentionLawful false and protestQuality above a threshold. The day-four threat must be classifiable by the player, with the classification affecting outcomes. Include a current-statute note on the IPC to BNS transition.

modules.title: When does influence become undue?
modules.doctrine: Domination of will plus unfair advantage; authority, fiduciary relations and mental distress.
modules.mechanic: play both adviser and vulnerable client and identify when assistance becomes domination.
modules.authority: Raghunath Prasad v Sarju Prasad, AIR 1924 PC 60
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three adviser-client transactions at differing prices and differing degrees of dependence. The player marks which are vitiated, and the reveal is that the transaction at the worst price is not the vitiated one because the client there was independent and well advised.
modules.lab: is played from the adviser's side, deliberately, because the compliance perspective teaches the doctrine better than the victim perspective and avoids modelling exploitation as gameplay. The player is a professional (the game lets them pick: a doctor, a lawyer, a spiritual teacher, a financial adviser) who has a genuine and legitimate opportunity to transact with a client, and whose objective is to complete the transaction in a form that will survive challenge. Dominance is largely given by the relationship and cannot be argued away, so the player's whole strategy must run through the second element and through the burden. Available moves are the real-world neutralisers, each with a cost and each only partially effective: insisting the client take independent legal advice (strong, slow, and the client may resent it), transacting at or above independent valuation (removes unfair advantage, reduces the adviser's benefit to near zero, which is the honest trade-off the game insists on), disclosing the adviser's own interest fully in writing, introducing a delay so the client can reconsider, and declining to act as adviser on the very matter in which they are transacting. The client's distress level, played by Claude, rises and falls with events, and transacting during a spike is fast and fatal. Round three brings a challenge by a family member under s 19A, and the court's power to set aside on terms means the player's outcome is not binary: a partially protected transaction may survive with a price adjustment, which rewards partial compliance and models real litigation. Failure mode is an adviser who documents consent meticulously while transacting at a bargain price during the client's worst week.
modules.win_loss: Win by completing a transaction that survives the s 19A challenge intact. A partial win exists where the court upholds it on adjusted terms. Lose instructively by relying on the client's enthusiastic written consent, which is precisely the evidence undue influence doctrine discounts.
modules.build_notes: Dominance is largely fixed by relationshipType and clientState, with only a small adviser-controllable component. UnfairAdvantage is computed from priceRatio and benefitAsymmetry. The s 19A outcome must have three states (upheld, set aside on terms, set aside absolutely) driven by how many neutralisers were present.

modules.title: Who must prove that the transaction was fair?
modules.doctrine: Unconscionable appearance, burden shifting and the court's power to set aside absolutely or on terms.
modules.mechanic: add relationship, price and disclosure evidence to competing scales until the burden shifts.
modules.authority: Subhas Chandra Das Mushib v Ganga Prosad Das Mushib, AIR 1967 SC 878
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: six facts are dealt and the player places them. The reveal shows that two facts moved the burden and four did not, and that one strong merits fact was played too early, before the burden had shifted, and was therefore wasted.
modules.lab: is a two-stage litigation. Stage one is the burden contest, played by the challenger with a limited hand. The player must reach the tipping point using only facts that bear on dominance and on the transaction appearing unconscionable, and here the design does something important: it withholds the merits facts from having any effect at this stage, so a player who leads with the most damning evidence of actual pressure finds the scale does not move, which is a faithful and surprising model of how s 16(3) works. Stage two flips the seats. If the burden has shifted, the player now defends and must positively prove the absence of undue influence, which is a different and much harder task than rebutting an allegation, and the game gives them a correspondingly harder resource position. Available defensive proofs are independent advice, full disclosure, the client's demonstrated understanding, and commercial justification for the terms, and each must be affirmatively established rather than merely asserted. Section 19A's power to set aside on terms means the defence can aim for a middle outcome. The strategic depth comes from stage-one decisions constraining stage two: a challenger who shifts the burden by emphasising the client's incapacity has also created a fact the defence can use to argue the client did not understand the very advice the defence relies on, which cuts both ways. Round three adds a settlement offer at the moment the burden shifts, whose value the player must assess against the cost of discharging it. Failure mode is a challenger who wins stage one spectacularly and finds the defendant discharges the burden with a single independent-advice letter.
modules.win_loss: Win as challenger by shifting the burden and surviving the discharge; win as defendant by discharging it or by achieving a set-aside-on-terms outcome that preserves most of the transaction. Lose instructively by spending merits evidence during the burden stage.
modules.build_notes: Tag each fact card with burdenWeight and meritsWeight independently; many cards should have zero in one field. Stage one must ignore meritsWeight entirely. The discharge stage requires affirmative proof objects, not rebuttals. Verify the current evidence-statute cross-reference before shipping.

modules.title: Was it a lie, concealment or a promise never intended to be kept?
modules.doctrine: Statutory forms of fraud, intention to deceive and distinction between later breach and fraudulent intention at formation.
modules.mechanic: inspect statements, internal messages and conduct to reconstruct the representor's intention.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a supplier promised a delivery date and missed it. The player is given three artefacts and asked whether this is fraud or breach. The reveal is that the answer depends entirely on one document's date, which is the module's central discipline.
modules.lab: is a twelve-artefact investigation with a discovery budget: the player can open only seven. Each artefact is described only by a label, so choosing what to open is a real judgment. The physics is that fraud lives at the moment of representation, so an internal report showing the supplier knew capacity was inadequate is devastating if dated before the promise and nearly worthless if dated after. The player learns to read the discovery list for dates rather than for content. Claude plays defence counsel with a policy of conceding the falsity of every statement (which is undeniable and does not matter) while asserting honest belief at the time, and then, if pressed on the unperformed promise, arguing that intention to perform existed and circumstances changed. That defence is genuinely strong and forces the player toward circumstantial proof: simultaneous representations to other buyers that contradict the one made to the client, a pattern of taking deposits with no corresponding procurement, a capacity commitment already fully allocated. Round three offers a choice with real consequences: pleading fraud opens rescission plus damages and carries reputational and evidentiary risk, while pleading breach is easier to prove and yields a smaller, contract-measured recovery. The player must choose before all artefacts are open. Round four introduces a second defendant whose knowledge is less clear, testing whether the player can allocate mental states to individuals rather than to a company as an undifferentiated whole. Failure mode is a player who assembles overwhelming evidence that the statement was false and never touches belief.
modules.win_loss: Win by establishing at least one s 17 limb with the mental state fixed at formation. Lose instructively by proving falsity and losing on belief, or by pleading fraud and having to fall back to breach after the limitation on amendment has bitten.
modules.build_notes: Every artefact carries a date and an attributableTo field. The fraud resolver must check date against representationDate and reject anything later. Attribution to individuals matters for the second defendant. The plead-fraud-or-breach choice should hard-branch before full information, and amendment should be time-limited.

modules.title: When does silence become fraudulent?
modules.anchor: ICA s 17 and its Explanation; s 19
modules.doctrine: No general duty to disclose, duty to speak, half-truths and silence equivalent to speech.
modules.mechanic: decide what to reveal in transactions involving changing facts, special relationships and misleading partial statements.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four known defects in a property. The player sets four switches and immediately sees which silences were lawful, which triggered a duty to speak, and which became fraudulent because of something the seller had already volunteered.
modules.lab: is a full sale negotiation over ten turns in which the player is the seller and new facts keep arriving. The core physics has three triggers, and the game makes the player discover each. First, the relationship trigger: where the parties stand in a relationship of trust, or where the seller has assumed to advise, a duty to speak arises and silence becomes fraud. Second, the half-truth trigger, which is the most instructive: once the seller says something partially true, silence about the remainder is no longer mere silence, so the very act of volunteering good news creates a duty to volunteer the bad. Third, the changed-circumstance trigger: a statement true when made and falsified by later events must be corrected before contracting, so a fact the seller disclosed accurately in turn two can become a fraud by turn eight without the seller saying another word. The strategic tension is that disclosure costs price and silence costs risk, and the buyer, played by Claude, asks probing questions designed to elicit half-truths, because a half-truth is far more valuable to a claimant than a pure silence. The sharpest decision arrives around turn six: the buyer asks a broad question that the player can answer narrowly and truthfully. Answering narrowly is technically accurate and creates precisely the half-truth that will sink the sale later; refusing to answer is lawful but signals a problem and drops the price; answering fully is safe and costs the most. Turn nine delivers a changed circumstance that falsifies an earlier true statement, and the player must decide whether to correct it days before completion. Failure mode is a seller who never lies once and is nonetheless liable under s 17 through the accumulation of accurate partial answers.
modules.win_loss: Win by completing the sale above the reserve price with no duty-to-speak breach outstanding at completion. Lose instructively by a truthful half-answer, or by failing to correct a statement overtaken by events.
modules.build_notes: Each fact object holds materiality, disclosedState and a dutyTrigger evaluated each turn against relationship, priorStatements and factChanges. The half-truth trigger must fire automatically when a partial disclosure overlaps a withheld fact. Show the trigger reason in the debrief, never during play.

modules.title: Was the false statement fraud or misrepresentation?
modules.doctrine: Innocent false assertion, breach of duty, causation, ordinary diligence and differences in remedies.
modules.mechanic: classify identical statements before and after evidence of the speaker's knowledge is revealed.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: one statement about a machine's output. The player classifies it with no knowledge evidence, then the internal test report appears and the classification changes. The reveal shows that the remedy changes with it.
modules.lab: is a claim-strategy exercise. The player's client bought a business on the strength of four statements, all false. Investigation reveals different mental states behind each: one made with knowledge, one made recklessly without warrant for the assertion, one made honestly on outdated information, one innocently causing a mistake as to the substance of the thing. The player must decide, for each, whether to plead fraud or misrepresentation, and the choices interact. The physics that drives the decisions is the s 19 proviso. Misrepresentation claims are exposed to the ordinary-diligence defence, and the business was sold with a data room the client could have searched, so Claude will run diligence hard on every misrepresentation count. Fraud counts are immune to that defence but require proof of the mental state, which is expensive. So the player faces a real allocation problem: spend investigative budget proving knowledge (converting counts to fraud and neutralising the diligence defence) or spend it proving that ordinary diligence would not have revealed the truth (preserving misrepresentation counts). Doing both on all four counts is impossible within budget. A further wrinkle: the remedies differ, and the client's actual objective (rescission and return of the purchase price, versus damages and keeping the business) should drive the choice, so the game makes the player interview the client and discover that the client wants to keep the business, which quietly makes rescission-focused strategy wrong. Failure mode is a player who pleads fraud on all four counts, fails the mental-state proof on three, and finds those counts cannot be salvaged as misrepresentation at that stage.
modules.win_loss: Win by recovering on at least two counts on the route matched to the client's actual objective. Lose instructively by pleading uniformly, or by winning rescission for a client who wanted to keep the business.
modules.build_notes: Each statement object holds actualMentalState (hidden), assertionWarrant, and discoverabilityByDiligence. The proviso must apply only to misrepresentation and s 17 silence counts. Client objective should be discoverable only through an interview action, so players who skip it make the classic error.

modules.title: What if both parties share the same essential factual mistake?
modules.doctrine: Bilateral mistake concerning a fact essential to the agreement, resulting voidness and restitution.
modules.mechanic: change one assumed fact - existence, title, quantity or identity - and watch the contract survive or collapse.
modules.authority: Tarsem Singh v Sukhminder Singh, (1998) 3 SCC 471
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player falsifies three assumptions in turn (the goods had already perished, the buyer already owned them, the goods were worth half what both thought). The reveal is that the third does not void the agreement, which is exactly what the Explanation says and exactly what learners expect it not to say.
modules.lab: places the player as counsel to a party who wants out of a completed transaction and has found a shared mistaken assumption. The strategy problem is twofold. First, characterisation: the assumption in question sits ambiguously between essence and quality, and the player must build the argument that it went to a matter of fact essential to the agreement rather than to value or to a collateral expectation. Available moves include establishing what the parties treated as fundamental in their negotiations, showing that the price was constructed on the assumption, and finding contemporaneous documents describing the subject matter by reference to the assumed fact. Second, and this is where the game earns its length, voidness is not a costless victory. Section 65 requires restoration, and the player's client has consumed part of the benefit, resold part of it, and improved the rest. The Restitution ledger updates live as the player builds their case, and around round three the player can see that a complete win under s 20 leaves the client worse off than a partial commercial settlement, because restoring benefits at present values is expensive. That confrontation is the module's point. Claude plays the counterparty with a policy of resisting the mistake argument while quietly preparing a large restitution counter-claim, which it deploys the moment the player commits. Round four adds a third-party purchaser whose position complicates restoration further. Failure mode is a player who wins on s 20 and hands the client a net loss.
modules.win_loss: Win by achieving the outcome with the best net position for the client, which may be a settlement rather than a declaration of voidness. Lose instructively by treating voidness as the objective rather than as one route to it.
modules.build_notes: Assumptions are typed as essential, quality or value, with the value type hard-wired to fail per the Explanation. The restitution ledger must compute live from consumption, resale and improvement records and be visible from turn one so the trade-off is legible throughout.

modules.title: What if only one party is mistaken, or the mistake concerns law?
modules.doctrine: Indian versus foreign law, unilateral mistake and exceptional mistakes concerning identity or the nature of a document.
modules.mechanic: transact with changing identities and documents and decide when unilateral mistake becomes legally material.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player tries to escape each of the four deals using unilateral mistake and finds that three routes are closed. The reveal introduces the s 72 contrast, which surprises learners who have just been told that mistake of law does not vitiate.
modules.lab: runs an identity fraud scenario in depth, because that is where the exception has real work to do. The player has sold high-value goods on credit to someone who represented themselves as an established firm. The goods have been resold to an innocent third party. The player's objective is recovery, and the legal question is whether the contract was void for mistake as to identity (in which case no title passed and the third party's position is exposed) or merely voidable for fraud (in which case the third party who bought in good faith before avoidance is protected). This is a genuinely difficult and genuinely valuable distinction, and the game builds the entire endgame on it. Investigation moves establish the facts that drive the characterisation: whether the player intended to deal with the named firm specifically or with the person in front of them, whether the identity was material to the decision to give credit, whether checks were made against the firm's actual details, and whether the dealing was face to face or at a distance. Each fact moves the characterisation, and the player can shape it partly by what they emphasise, which is the interpretive axis operating on facts rather than on words. Meanwhile a clock runs, because the third party is about to resell again, and Claude plays their counsel with a policy of stressing the face-to-face elements to force a fraud characterisation. Round three offers a settlement from the third party priced at the midpoint, and the player must judge their own characterisation's strength. A parallel thread runs the mistake-of-law deal, where the contract cannot be avoided under s 21 but a payment made under it may be recoverable under s 72, and the player must notice that the two provisions coexist. Failure mode is a player who pursues unilateral mistake on the ordinary deals and exhausts the budget before reaching the identity claim.
modules.win_loss: Win by recovering the goods or their value from the third party on a sustainable characterisation, plus the s 72 payment. Lose instructively by treating s 22 as a general escape, or by conceding a fraud characterisation and losing priority to the innocent purchaser.
modules.build_notes: Identity characterisation resolves from a weighted fact set (intentionToDealWith, materialityOfIdentity, checksMade, dealingMode) into void or voidable, and that single flag must drive third-party title. Keep the s 72 thread on an independent resolver so the coexistence is visible.

modules.title: Are the consideration and object lawful?
modules.doctrine: Separating consideration from object and applying the statutory categories of unlawfulness.
modules.mechanic: inspect the payment, promised act and ultimate purpose separately before issuing an enforceability result.
modules.authority: Gherulal Parakh v Mahadeodas Maiya, AIR 1959 SC 781
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three transactions run through the scanner. A lawful sale of a lawful chemical to a buyer who has stated an unlawful use; an unlawful payment for a lawful service; an ordinary commercial supply. The reveal is the independence of the two chambers.
modules.lab: puts the player in a compliance role at a chemicals and equipment distributor. Twelve orders arrive over four weeks, each with a stated purpose, a price structure and a customer profile. The player must approve, refuse or approve with conditions, under a revenue target that makes blanket refusal a losing strategy. The physics is that s 23 bites on the object, so knowledge of the customer's purpose is legally material, which creates the game's central and uncomfortable mechanic: investigating purpose can destroy a sale by giving the seller knowledge it would rather not have. That mechanic drives the strategy. The player can approve quickly on a clean face, which maximises revenue and leaves them exposed if the purpose surfaces later, or investigate, which protects them but slows the pipeline and occasionally reveals a purpose that forces refusal of an otherwise profitable order. Approving with conditions (end-use certificates, restrictions on resale) is a middle path that costs less than refusal, and the game rewards players who work out which orders it suits. Week three introduces the fraudulent-consideration limb, where the price structure itself is the problem: an order priced to disguise a payment, which is unlawful in the consideration chamber even though the goods and the purpose are entirely legitimate. Week four brings an audit that tests every approved order against both chambers. Failure mode is a compliance officer who scrutinises purposes rigorously and approves a set of transactions whose payment structures are themselves unlawful.
modules.win_loss: Win by hitting the revenue target with zero orders failing the audit in either chamber. Lose instructively by scanning only one chamber, or by adopting a see-no-evil approval policy that collapses when purpose evidence surfaces.
modules.build_notes: Two independent resolver functions over the same transaction object, each returning a triggered category or null. Enforceability is the logical AND. knowledgeOfPurpose must be a mutable flag set by investigation actions, and the object resolver must depend on it, so the player can feel the perverse incentive and discuss it in the debrief.

modules.title: Does the agreement break or defeat the law indirectly?
modules.doctrine: Express statutory prohibition, arrangements defeating statutory policy and fraudulent transactions.
modules.mechanic: attempt to reach a commercial objective through different routes while the law detects prohibited circumvention.
modules.authority: Mannalal Khetan v Kedar Nath Khetan, (1977) 2 SCC 424
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player is given an objective blocked by a direct prohibition and three routes around it. They pick one and see whether it survives. The reveal is that the route with the most steps was not the safest, because its steps had no independent rationale.
modules.lab: runs a structuring engagement across four rounds. The player advises a client who wants an outcome that a statute prohibits directly, and must design a structure. Each structural step costs money and time, and each may be given an independent commercial rationale at additional cost. The physics is the second limb of s 23: a structure fails not because it is complicated but because its object is to defeat the statute, and independent rationale for each step is the principal thing that breaks the Purpose Trace. Claude plays a regulator with an investigation budget, and its policy is to follow the Purpose Trace, opening the step with the weakest independent rationale first. This produces a genuine arms race: the player can add steps (which lengthens the trace and may look worse), buy rationale (expensive, and only credible if the step genuinely does something), or abandon the objective and pursue a lawful alternative that delivers eighty per cent of the value, which is available from round one and which most players ignore until they have burned their budget. That option is deliberately present, because recognising when structuring is not worth it is the professional skill the module is really teaching. Round three adds a whistleblower who supplies the regulator with the client's internal instruction describing the object of the structure in plain words, which is the single most common way such schemes fail and which no amount of external rationale repairs. Failure mode is an elegant structure destroyed by one internal email.
modules.win_loss: Win by achieving the objective (or the lawful eighty per cent alternative) with the structure surviving the regulator's investigation. Lose instructively by building a structure whose internal record states its object.
modules.build_notes: Each step object holds independentRationaleStrength and a link to the ultimate objective. Purpose Trace strength is computed as objective linkage minus aggregate rationale. The regulator is a search function over weakest links with a budget. The lawful alternative must be visible and quantified from the start.

modules.title: When do injury, immorality or public policy defeat a bargain?
modules.doctrine: Injury to person or property, immorality and judicially controlled public-policy categories.
modules.mechanic: decide difficult agreements using limited precedent cards rather than unrestricted moral intuition.
modules.authority: Gherulal Parakh v Mahadeodas Maiya, AIR 1959 SC 781
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three agreements are presented and the player decides each using only the cards in hand. One agreement is repugnant and no card fits, which is the intended discomfort and the point of the module.
modules.lab: runs a docket of eight cases over three sittings, and the design gives the player two competing objectives that cannot both be maximised: decide the cases justly, and keep the Legitimacy meter high, which means keeping public policy tethered to precedent. Several cases are morally straightforward and doctrinally unsupported, and the player must decide whether to reach for a new head. Creating a new head is permitted, costs Legitimacy immediately, and adds a card to the hand that becomes available for later cases in the docket, so an early expansion pays off later if the player can live with the cost. The engine that makes this a genuine strategy game is that Claude plays counsel on both sides and, crucially, plays a later litigant who invokes the player's own new head in a case where it produces a result the player dislikes. That is the structural lesson: a head of public policy created to strike down an oppressive employment term will be cited next week to strike down a commercial arbitration clause, and the player must live with it. The Gherulal and Brojo Nath tension is presented directly as two cards the player may lead with, one narrow and one expansive, and each shapes the remaining docket differently. Sitting three delivers a case squarely between them, and the player's earlier choices have already constrained what they can say. Failure mode is a player who expands generously in sitting one and finds by sitting three that public policy has become a general fairness power they can no longer control.
modules.win_loss: Win by clearing the docket with defensible outcomes and Legitimacy above the floor. Lose instructively by expanding public policy so far that the doctrine loses shape, or by refusing to expand at all and enforcing a plainly unconscionable adhesion term.
modules.build_notes: Precedent cards are data with matchStrength functions against case attributes. New heads must be creatable and must persist into later cases in the same run, and Claude must actively cite them. Legitimacy is a running score, not a pass or fail. Present the doctrinal split explicitly in the debrief.

modules.title: Can the lawful part of a mixed bargain be saved?
modules.doctrine: Indivisible unlawful consideration, severable reciprocal promises and alternative promises with an illegal branch.
modules.mechanic: remove or separate unlawful promises without rewriting the parties' bargain.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the same three obligations are shown in three different architectures, one of which loses everything under s 24 and one of which loses only the tainted promise under s 57. The reveal is that the difference is drafting, not substance.
modules.lab: is played in two phases and the second phase is the payoff. In phase one the player drafts a complex agreement with eight obligations, choosing the architecture: which obligations share a single consideration, which are structured as separate reciprocal sets, and which are framed as alternatives. Every architectural choice has a commercial cost, because separating promises into distinct sets weakens the linkage the client wants (they want the counterparty unable to take one benefit without the other), and alternatives create optionality the counterparty may exploit. In phase two, one obligation turns out to be unlawful, and the player discovers which only after drafting is locked. Now the architecture they built determines what survives. If the tainted obligation shared a single consideration with the rest, s 24 takes everything, which is the catastrophic outcome the module exists to prevent. If it sat in a separate reciprocal set, s 57 saves the rest. If it was one branch of an alternative, s 58 leaves the lawful branch enforceable. Because the player did not know which obligation would be tainted, the drafting phase is a real hedging problem: separating everything is maximally safe and commercially useless, so they must judge which obligations carry the most illegality risk. Round three adds a second taint, testing whether the architecture was robust or merely lucky, and a salvage phase lets the player attempt post-hoc separation, which the game largely refuses because s 24 looks at the consideration as it was structured. Failure mode is a beautifully integrated contract in which every promise supports every other and one taint destroys all eight.
modules.win_loss: Win by retaining at least six of eight obligations after both taints, with the commercial linkage score above threshold. Lose instructively by achieving perfect linkage and losing the whole agreement to s 24.
modules.build_notes: Represent the agreement as a graph of promises with consideration groupings. Implement ss 24, 57 and 58 as three distinct resolvers over that graph. Taints are assigned after the drafting phase is locked. Post-hoc severance attempts should fail where the consideration grouping is single, with the reason shown.

modules.title: Can a contract restrict marriage or trade?
modules.doctrine: Void restraints, the statutory goodwill exception and distinguishing restraint from legitimate protection of confidential interests.
modules.mechanic: design restrictions for an employee or business seller and test how far each clause goes.
modules.authority: Gujarat Bottling Co Ltd v Coca Cola Co, (1995) 5 SCC 545; Niranjan Shankar Golikari v Century Spinning, AIR 1967 SC 1098
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player drafts one non-compete and drags it across the termination line, watching the Enforceability light change without a word of the clause changing. The reveal is that Indian law's dividing line is temporal, not qualitative, which is the opposite of what learners trained on English or American materials expect.
modules.lab: is a protection problem, not a drafting exercise, and that reframing is the module's contribution. The player runs a specialist consultancy whose senior employee is leaving to join a competitor, and whose real assets are client relationships, a proprietary methodology and a pricing model. The instinctive move, a two-year non-compete, is void under s 27 and the game says so immediately, forcing the player to find the actual protections available. Those protections are the game's content, and each has a cost and a limit. Confidentiality obligations survive termination because protecting confidential information is not a restraint on trade, but they only reach information that is genuinely confidential, so the player must have classified it in advance, and doing so during the notice period is too late. Garden leave and long notice periods operate during the subsistence of the contract and are therefore outside s 27 under the Golikari line, but they are expensive, since the employer pays for months of non-work. Client contracts can be structured so that the relationship belongs to the firm, which is a pre-emptive move made years earlier. The goodwill exception under s 27 is available if the departure is structured as a sale of the employee's interest, which changes the commercial deal entirely. Claude plays the departing employee's counsel, who tests each protection and, crucially, argues that the confidentiality clause is a restraint in disguise where it is drawn so broadly that compliance would prevent the employee working at all, which is a real and important line. Round three has the employee already at the competitor and the player choosing which protection to enforce, knowing that a failed injunction application signals weakness to the rest of the workforce. Failure mode is a firm holding a well-drafted, entirely void two-year non-compete.
modules.win_loss: Win by preserving client retention and confidential information above thresholds without relying on a void restraint. Lose instructively by seeking to enforce the non-compete, or by drafting confidentiality so broadly that it is struck down as a restraint.
modules.build_notes: Zone (during term or post term) must be the first check in the enforceability resolver, and the resolver must state the zone rule explicitly. Confidentiality clauses need a breadthScore that can tip them into restraint territory. Model garden leave as a cost, not a free move.

modules.title: Can a contract prevent a party from approaching a court?
modules.anchor: ICA s 28; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, s 7
modules.doctrine: Absolute restraints, clauses extinguishing rights or discharging liability and valid arbitration agreements.
modules.mechanic: approve, redraft or reject litigation bans, shortened claim periods and arbitration provisions.
modules.authority: Hakam Singh v Gammon (India) Ltd, (1971) 1 SCC 286
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player reviews four clauses and marks each valid or void. The reveal is that the clause naming one of several competent courts is valid (it selects among available forums rather than ousting jurisdiction), while the innocuous-looking thirty-day claim clause is void as extinguishing a right.
modules.lab: is a redrafting engagement. The player's client is a service provider facing a long tail of small claims and wants them to stop. The client's proposed clause, which the player is handed, is void several times over, and the player must deliver a package that achieves as much of the commercial objective as s 28 permits, defending each element against Claude playing opposing counsel in a later dispute. The available moves map the actual law. Arbitration is permitted under Exception 1 and delivers privacy and finality, but it costs money per claim and, for small claims, may cost the client more than the claims themselves, so it solves the wrong problem. A tiered clause requiring notification and negotiation before proceedings is valid if it does not operate as an absolute bar, and the player must find the drafting line between a condition precedent (permissible) and a trap that extinguishes the right (void). Contractual limitation of the time for making a claim is void under s 28, but a notification requirement that preserves the right while regulating process may survive, and distinguishing these two is the module's hardest and most valuable exercise. A clause limiting the quantum of liability is not a s 28 problem at all, and belongs to Module 50, which the game points to; recognising which module a problem belongs to is itself a scored skill here. Round three tests the package in a live dispute where the counterparty missed the notification deadline, and the player discovers whether their clause bars the claim or merely embarrasses it. Failure mode is a player who converts every element into arbitration and hands the client a dispute system more expensive than the claims it was meant to control.
modules.win_loss: Win by delivering a package that survives challenge and reduces the client's dispute cost below target. Lose instructively by drafting a notification requirement that crosses into extinguishment, or by solving the problem with arbitration the client cannot afford.
modules.build_notes: Each clause element is classified by a resolver into permissible process regulation, time limitation (void), right extinguishment (void) or absolute restriction (void), with arbitration handled by the exception path. Cost modelling per claim type is essential, otherwise the arbitration trade-off is invisible.

modules.title: Can a court rescue a vague bargain?
modules.doctrine: Uncertainty, ascertainability, ambiguous language, missing standards and impermissible judicial reconstruction.
modules.mechanic: supply objective mechanisms such as market price or third-party valuation without inventing a new contract.
modules.authority: Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel v Lalbhai Trikumlal Mills Ltd, AIR 1958 SC 512
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the same term is expressed three ways ('price to be agreed', 'price at the prevailing market rate on the delivery date as published by a named exchange', 'a fair price'). The player marks each, and the reveal shows that only the second is safely enforceable and explains why the third is genuinely arguable.
modules.lab: is a long-term supply negotiation in which the parties genuinely cannot fix all four terms, because the contract runs for five years across a volatile input market. The player must keep the deal certain enough to enforce and flexible enough to be worth signing, and the two objectives are in direct opposition, which is the engine of the game. Every machinery choice costs flexibility, and every open term costs enforceability. Three complications create depth. First, machinery can fail: the named index is discontinued in year three, and the player discovers whether they drafted a fallback, which is a move available cheaply at drafting time and impossible afterwards. Second, machinery that depends on one party's determination raises a different question, since a determination clause is capable of being made certain only if it is constrained by an objective standard, and Claude will argue that an unconstrained discretion leaves the term uncertain and takes the whole agreement with it under s 29. Third, the interaction with Module 47 is live: a court supplying an implied term is doing something different from enforcing machinery, and the player must not confuse the two, because implication cannot cure a term the parties expressly left to future agreement. Round three delivers a dispute where the counterparty argues the agreement is void for uncertainty, and the value at stake is the entire five-year contract, so the drafting decisions made in round one are now worth a great deal. Failure mode is a player who leaves price to be agreed in exchange for a strong commercial concession elsewhere, and finds the concession sits in a void agreement.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending five years with the contract enforceable throughout and flexibility above the client's minimum. Lose instructively by leaving a term to future agreement, or by installing machinery so rigid that the client abandons the contract commercially in year two.
modules.build_notes: Each term holds a mechanism object with objectivity (0 to 3) and fallback (nullable). Certainty resolves from objectivity; a mechanism failure event in year three tests fallback. Flexibility is inversely weighted to objectivity so the trade-off is structural rather than cosmetic.

modules.title: Is the transaction a wager or a contingent contract?
modules.doctrine: Mutual chance of gain or loss versus a genuine contract dependent on a collateral uncertain event; happening, non-happening, time and impossibility.
modules.mechanic: compare a cricket bet with weather-dependent supply and event-cancellation agreements.
modules.authority: Gherulal Parakh v Mahadeodas Maiya, AIR 1959 SC 781
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player classifies three instruments. The reveal is that insurance and a wager have identical payout structures and are distinguished only by insurable interest, which is exactly the test the module exists to teach.
modules.lab: is a structuring and enforcement game across three rounds. The player runs a trading desk and must build a book of instruments that hedge real exposures while remaining enforceable. The physics is that a wager is void and unenforceable in the courts, so an unenforceable instrument in the book is a hole in the hedge that only appears when the counterparty declines to pay, which the game arranges to happen at the worst moment. The strategic decisions are about interest and settlement. An instrument settled by physical delivery is hard to characterise as a wager; one settled in differences with no underlying position looks much more like one, so the player must decide whether to take real positions (expensive, capital-intensive) or to rely on documentation of intent. Round two introduces the collateral transaction question: the desk has borrowed to fund positions, and if the underlying instruments were wagers, the player must determine whether the loans are affected, which under Gherulal Parakh they generally are not, but which changes where state law makes wagering illegal rather than merely void. The game therefore includes a jurisdiction variable and requires the player to check it, which is the kind of thing that is invisible in a national-level treatment and decisive in practice. Round three brings a defaulting counterparty who pleads s 30, and the player must defend the characterisation of each affected instrument using the interest and structure evidence they built earlier. Failure mode is a desk that is perfectly hedged in economic terms and holds three void instruments.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending the book hedged with all instruments enforceable and the collateral funding intact. Lose instructively by relying on a differences-settled instrument with no underlying interest, or by assuming the collateral loans fall with the wagers when they do not.
modules.build_notes: Each instrument holds underlyingInterest (boolean), settlementMode, and reciprocalExposure. Classification resolves from those three. A jurisdiction flag switches wagering from void to illegal and cascades to collateral contracts. Make the cascade visible, since that is the teaching point.

modules.title: Was the statement a term, representation, sales puff or essential promise?
modules.doctrine: Classification affects rescission, termination and damages; relevance of expertise, reliance, timing and importance.
modules.mechanic: sort statements made during a product demonstration and then choose the available remedy.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player classifies four statements and sees the remedies that follow. The reveal is that the statement the buyer cared about most yields nothing because it was a projection of future performance framed as opinion by an expert seller, which is precisely where the doctrine bites hardest.
modules.lab: is a claim-building exercise in which the player must reverse-engineer from the client's objective. The client bought a production line, wants to give it back and recover the price, and the player must find a route to termination rather than to damages. That objective is only reachable through a condition or an essential promise going to the root, or through rescission for misrepresentation, and the two have different requirements and different obstacles. The moves available are evidentiary and rhetorical. The player can establish the seller's superior expertise (which pushes statements toward terms rather than representations), demonstrate the buyer's reliance, show that the statement was the reason the buyer chose this seller over another, and show that the written contract's silence on the point was the seller's doing. Against that, the contract contains an entire agreement provision, and Claude will argue that anything not written in is at most a representation, so the player must decide whether to attack that provision or to work around it by pleading misrepresentation, which the provision cannot exclude in the same way. The sharpest decision arrives when the player realises that pleading fraud (Module 33) would defeat both the entire agreement provision and the diligence proviso, but requires proving the seller's knowledge, which the investigation budget may not stretch to. Round three introduces the timing question under s 55, since delay in rejecting the line may have converted a right to terminate into a right to damages only, so the player must also account for what their own client did after discovery. Failure mode is a player who proves the statements false, secures damages, and delivers a client still stuck with an unusable production line.
modules.win_loss: Win by achieving termination and price recovery. A partial win is damages sufficient to replace the line. Lose instructively by winning on classification routes that yield only damages when the client needed to get out.
modules.build_notes: Each statement carries expertise, reliance, temporalProximity, writtenIncorporation and importance. A classifier maps these to puff, representation, warranty or condition, and a remedy table maps classification to outcomes. The entire agreement provision must be a modelled obstacle with defined ways around it.

modules.title: What did the parties promise expressly or by implication?
modules.anchor: ICA ss 9, 29, 37; implication is case-law based
modules.doctrine: Express and implied-in-fact obligations, business necessity and the boundary between completing and rewriting a bargain.
modules.mechanic: decide whether missing obligations are necessary, obvious or merely desirable.
modules.authority: Nabha Power Ltd v Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd, (2018) 11 SCC 508
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three proposed implied terms are tested. One is necessary (without it the contract cannot operate at all), one is obvious, one is merely sensible. The reveal is that the third fails, and that most terms clients want implied fall into the third category.
modules.lab: is a dispute over a facilities management contract that is silent on several operationally critical points. The player acts for the client and must select which gaps to litigate, with a budget permitting three. Each gap has a different profile: one is necessary for business efficacy and cheap to argue but worth little; one is worth a great deal and only reasonable, so it will fail; one is obvious but arguably contradicted by an express provision elsewhere, which is fatal because implication cannot override an express term. The mechanic that makes this a strategy game is that arguing for an implied term is not free of consequences. Claude, for the counterparty, will accept implication in principle and propose a version of the term less favourable to the player's client, because a court supplying a term supplies the minimum necessary rather than the client's preferred version. So the player who wins implication may lose the point, and must weigh whether to argue implication at all or to argue instead that the contract's silence should be construed against the drafter, which is Module 49's territory and is available as a cross-move. Round two introduces a course of dealing between the parties over several previous contracts, which supports implication in fact and is powerful, but which also imports terms the client would rather not have, since a course of dealing works in both directions. Round three tests whether the player's implied terms survive alongside the express machinery, and the failure mode is a client who succeeds in implying a term and finds the court's version of it worse than no term at all.
modules.win_loss: Win by securing at least two implied terms whose court-supplied content still delivers the commercial objective. Lose instructively by spending the budget on the valuable-but-merely-reasonable gap, or by winning a term whose minimum content is useless.
modules.build_notes: Each gap holds efficacyNecessity, obviousness, expressContradiction and clientValue. Implication resolves on necessity or obviousness, never on reasonableness, and must produce a courtVersion of the term that is deliberately minimal. Course of dealing should import a fixed bundle of terms, both helpful and unhelpful.

modules.title: Did the hidden standard terms become part of the contract?
modules.anchor: ICA ss 10, 13-14; CPA s 2(46); case law
modules.doctrine: Signature, timing and sufficiency of notice, previous dealings and meaningful assent to unusual terms.
modules.mechanic: locate terms before payment, after payment and behind links, then determine which were incorporated.
modules.authority: Bharati Knitting Co v DHL Worldwide Express Courier Division, (1996) 4 SCC 704
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: one onerous term is placed at four positions in turn. The reveal is that position alone flips it between incorporated and not, and that a term placed correctly may still fail because its onerousness demanded greater prominence.
modules.lab: is played as a designer first and a consumer advocate second. As designer, the player runs a parking and events business and must incorporate six terms of varying onerousness, subject to a conversion constraint: every prominence increase reduces sales, and moving terms earlier in the flow increases abandonment. The physics has two dials that interact, timing and prominence, and the requirement scales with onerousness, so an ordinary term can sit quietly on a ticket while a term excluding liability for personal injury needs something close to a signature. The course-of-dealing mechanic adds a third dimension the player can invest in: with repeat customers, consistent prior dealings can incorporate terms without fresh notice, which is cheap and powerful but requires consistency the player must maintain across the whole customer base, and one inconsistent transaction damages it. In the second half the player switches to advocate for a customer injured by an incorporated term, and attacks along three lines: timing (the term arrived after the contract was made), prominence (an onerous term buried), and the s 23 and CPA overlay from Brojo Nath (the term is unconscionable in a standard form contract regardless of incorporation). The last of these is the important structural insight, because it means incorporation is not the end of the enquiry, and a player who wins on incorporation as designer can still lose on unconscionability. Round three brings a regulator reviewing the flow as a whole. Failure mode is a designer who achieves perfect incorporation of a term that is then struck down as unconscionable, having paid the full conversion cost for nothing.
modules.win_loss: Win as designer by incorporating at least four of six terms with conversion above target and none struck down; win as advocate by defeating the term on any of the three lines. Lose instructively by giving notice after the contracting moment, however prominently.
modules.build_notes: The flow is an ordered array with a contractingMoment index. Incorporation resolves on position, prominence and a requiredProminence derived from onerousness. Validity is a separate downstream resolver applying s 23 and CPA unfairness. Keep them visibly separate in the interface.

modules.title: Which interpretation of the words should control?
modules.anchor: ICA ss 9, 29; CPA s 2(46); interpretive case law
modules.doctrine: Text, context, commercial purpose, ambiguity, contra proferentem and distinction between interpretation and implication.
modules.mechanic: choose between literal, contextual and commercially plausible readings and justify the selection.
modules.authority: General Assurance Society Ltd v Chandmull Jain, AIR 1966 SC 1644; Nabha Power Ltd v PSPCL, (2018) 11 SCC 508
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: one indemnity clause read three ways, producing three different exposures. The player picks the reading that favours their client and then discovers that the same reading, applied to a second clause in the same contract, hurts them, which is the consistency constraint the module is built on.
modules.lab: is a dispute with four clauses in play, and the constraint that makes it a game is consistency: an advocate who argues literalism on clause one and commercial purpose on clause three will be held to the inconsistency by Claude, whose policy is to quote the player's own submissions back at them. So the player must choose an interpretive posture for the case as a whole and then find the best result available within it, which is exactly the discipline appellate advocates operate under. Three further mechanics deepen this. First, contra proferentem is available only against the proposer, and the player must establish who proposed each clause, which is an evidential move with a cost, and which may reveal that their own client proposed two of the four. Second, extrinsic material (prior drafts, negotiation correspondence) is available at a cost and cuts both ways, so a player who opens the negotiation record to support a contextual reading may hand the counterparty a better reading of a different clause. Third, the boundary with implication is policed: where the player's contextual reading is really an attempt to add a term, the court will say so and the argument fails, which forces precision about whether the words used can bear the meaning proposed. Round three delivers the counterparty's opening submission, and the player must decide whether to hold their posture or switch, knowing that switching costs credibility and that holding may cost the point. Failure mode is a player who wins three clauses on a literal approach and loses the fourth, which happens to be the valuable one, to the same approach.
modules.win_loss: Win by achieving the best aggregate value across all four clauses within one consistent posture. Lose instructively by winning individual clauses through incompatible arguments and being held to the contradiction.
modules.build_notes: Each clause holds three precomputed outcomes with strength scores against the available material. A postureConsistency tracker must penalise switching, and Claude must literally quote earlier player submissions. Extrinsic material should be a shared pool: opening it benefits both sides.

modules.title: Can a business exclude liability or impose a one-sided term?
modules.doctrine: Exemption and limitation clauses, fundamental obligations and statutory nullification of unfair consumer terms.
modules.mechanic: redline deposits, penalties, unilateral termination, assignment and liability exclusions.
modules.authority: Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd v Govindan Raghavan, (2019) 5 SCC 725
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four terms are redlined by the player and the reveal shows that the term most people delete first (a broad liability cap) survives, while an innocuous-looking unilateral variation clause is the most vulnerable.
modules.lab: is a two-sided engagement. In the first half the player is in-house counsel drafting the terms for a subscription service, with a Business Value target that cannot be met by deleting everything risky. They must therefore find the versions of each term that retain most of the value at least risk: a liability cap at a defensible multiple rather than a total exclusion, termination rights that are reciprocal or tied to defined causes rather than unilateral and unreasoned, a deposit proportionate to actual risk rather than punitive, and assignment rights that do not prejudice the consumer. In the second half the same contract is attacked, and the player switches to consumer counsel. Now the three routes matter distinctly: CPA unfairness has a defined statutory test and a forum with power to declare terms void; s 23 public policy under the Brojo Nath line reaches unconscionable terms in standard form contracts even outside the consumer relationship but demands a higher showing; s 28 reaches terms that restrict enforcement of rights, including short claim windows, and is a different attack entirely because it does not require unfairness at all. Choosing the route determines which facts matter, and running the wrong one wastes the strongest evidence. Claude defends by disputing the consumer characterisation on one contract (a business subscriber), which closes the CPA route and forces the player onto s 23, where the standard is harder. Round three introduces a regulator considering a class-wide direction, so the player must think about which term is worst across the population rather than worst for their individual client. Failure mode is an attacker who runs the CPA route against a non-consumer and loses the case on characterisation before reaching the merits.
modules.win_loss: Win as drafter by hitting Business Value with aggregate exposure under threshold; win as attacker by striking at least three terms on correctly chosen routes. Lose instructively by drafting a total exclusion of liability for a fundamental obligation, or by attacking on a route the relationship does not support.
modules.build_notes: Each term carries three independent risk scores keyed to route. Consumer status is an attribute of the relationship, not the term, and must gate the CPA route. The regulator phase should evaluate the term set across a simulated population rather than one claimant.

modules.title: Did the user genuinely consent online?
modules.anchor: ICA ss 3-9, 13-19; IT Act ss 4, 5, 10A-13; CPA ss 2(46)-(47); CCPA Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023
modules.doctrine: Clickwrap, browsewrap, pre-ticked boxes, subscription traps, automated attribution and the gap between formal and meaningful assent.
modules.mechanic: make the same purchase through neutral and manipulative interfaces and compare contractual outcomes.
modules.authority: Trimex International FZE Ltd v Vedanta Aluminium Ltd, (2010) 3 SCC 1
sources: Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player runs one purchase through each flow and compares what they bought, what they agreed to, and what it cost. The reveal is that both flows produced formally valid contracts and only one produced anything resembling real assent.
modules.lab: is a full product design cycle with a revenue target and a regulatory exposure limit, which is precisely the trade-off real product teams face. The player designs a checkout with twelve design decisions: default states of consent boxes, placement and prominence of the total price, the cancellation path for a subscription, urgency signalling, the wording of the decline option, and the point at which terms are presented (which is Module 48's timing dial, now in a digital context). Each dark pattern raises revenue measurably and adds exposure to the register. The physics runs on three layers at once, and the module's contribution is showing that they can give different answers. Formation under IT Act s 10A is easy to satisfy: a click is an acceptance, and attribution rules under s 11 make it stick. Vitiation under ss 14 to 19 is harder for the consumer to establish, because a pre-ticked box or a confusing flow is not obviously fraud or misrepresentation, and this gap is the reason the CCPA Guidelines exist. The Guidelines themselves operate as consumer protection enforcement rather than contract law, so a design can produce a valid contract, survive a vitiation challenge, and still be an unfair trade practice attracting CCPA action, which is the layered result the player must navigate. Round three brings an enforcement notice targeting three specific elements, and the player must decide which to remove, knowing the revenue cost of each. Round four gives the player the consumer's side in a specific dispute over an unwanted subscription renewal, where the strongest argument turns out to be the subscription-trap classification rather than anything in the ICA. Failure mode is a designer who satisfies contract law perfectly and collects an enforcement action, which is the actual state of much of the Indian market.
modules.win_loss: Win by hitting the revenue target with the Dark Pattern register clear of the specified thirteen and formation robust. Lose instructively by optimising conversion into an enforcement action, or by stripping the flow so thoroughly that revenue collapses without any corresponding legal gain.
modules.build_notes: Three independent resolvers over the same flow object: formationValid (IT Act), vitiationRisk (ICA), darkPatternRegister (CCPA list of thirteen). Never merge them. Each design decision carries a revenueDelta and register entries. Keep the pattern list as configurable data since the CCPA may modify Annexure I.

modules.title: Who must perform, and who bears a joint promise?
modules.doctrine: Personal performance, accepted third-party performance, joint liability, contribution, release and devolution of rights and liabilities.
modules.mechanic: allocate unfinished tasks and losses among several promisors without using agency principles.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the promisee sues one solvent promisor for the whole loss. The player predicts whether that is permitted, and the reveal is that it is under s 43, and that the burden of pursuing the others then falls on the promisor who paid.
modules.lab: is played from the promisor's chair, which is where the strategy lives. The player is one of four joint promisors on a failed project, and is the most solvent, which means the promisee will come for them first. Their objective is to minimise net exposure across three rounds, and the tools are all found in ss 42 to 45. The decisions are genuinely difficult. Should the player perform early and voluntarily, which caps the loss and preserves the relationship but starts the contribution problem from the largest possible base? Should they negotiate a release from the promisee, which under s 44 does not discharge the others and may therefore be obtainable more cheaply than the player expects, since the promisee loses less by releasing one than intuition suggests? Should they seek an express agreement varying s 43's default before the claim crystallises, which is cheap now and impossible later? Round two introduces the insolvency of one promisor, and s 43's rule that the default is shared equally among the remaining promisors converts a third party's failure into the player's cost, which is the moment most players understand joint liability properly. Round three tests personal performance under s 40: one obligation was of a kind the promisee was entitled to have performed by a specific promisor, so substituting another does not discharge it, and the player must identify which obligation that was. Failure mode is a player who settles generously with the promisee and then finds the contribution claims against their co-promisors worthless.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending with net exposure below the player's proportionate fault share. Lose instructively by paying the whole and recovering nothing in contribution, or by relying on a co-promisor to discharge an obligation that required personal performance.
modules.build_notes: Model joint promisors as a set with solvency, faultShare and releaseState. Section 43 recovery must permit full recovery from any one; contribution must redistribute per the statutory default including the equal-sharing rule on default. Section 44 must expressly not discharge the others. Section 40 personal performance is a flag on specific obligations.

modules.title: Was a valid offer of performance made?
modules.doctrine: Complete and unconditional tender, proper time, place and manner, and neglect by the promisee to provide facilities.
modules.mechanic: coordinate payment, access, location and tender while one party obstructs performance.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three attempted deliveries are shown, each failing on a different element of s 38 (one conditional on immediate payment, one at the wrong place, one giving no opportunity to inspect). The reveal is that all three leave the risk with the seller.
modules.lab: runs a delivery under obstruction over five days. The buyer, played by Claude, wants the seller to fail, and its policy is to obstruct in ways that look like ordinary commercial friction: no one available to receive, an insistence on a different location, a refusal to provide access to the unloading bay, and a demand for documents not required by the contract. The player must respond in a way that either completes performance or produces a valid tender, and the difference is worth the entire contract. The decisions map the statutory elements directly. Attaching any condition to the tender destroys it under s 38, so a seller who offers to deliver on immediate payment where the contract allows credit has not tendered at all, and the temptation to attach that condition is deliberately strong because the buyer looks likely to default. Delivering outside the contractual window fails on time, but s 47 and s 48 give the player room where the contract specifies a day but not an hour, and the player must read the contract to find it. Section 67 is the module's most valuable weapon: where the buyer refuses reasonable facilities, the player is excused, but only if they can show they sought those facilities and were refused, which requires generating a record in real time rather than arguing afterwards. Day four presents the sharpest choice, when the buyer offers to accept delivery at a different place at the player's cost, and the player must decide whether accepting preserves the relationship at a cost, or whether refusing and tendering at the contractual place is legally stronger and commercially fatal. Failure mode is a seller who does everything commercially sensible, ends up with the goods still in the warehouse, and cannot show a valid tender.
modules.win_loss: Win by completing delivery or by establishing a valid tender that transfers the risk. Lose instructively by attaching a protective condition to the tender, which is the most common and most costly error under s 38.
modules.build_notes: Tender validity is a conjunctive check over unconditional, timing, place and inspectionOpportunity, and each failure must be named. Section 67 excuse requires a facilitiesRequested record predating the refusal. Obstruction events are scripted with an escalation curve.

modules.title: Which reciprocal promise must be performed first?
modules.doctrine: Concurrent and sequential promises, readiness and willingness, prevention and default in the promise that should occur first.
modules.mechanic: contractor, owner and supplier cannot move until the legally prior obligation is performed.
modules.authority: Nathulal v Phoolchand, AIR 1970 SC 546
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: two obligations are due and neither party will move. The player must determine who is obliged to go first, and the reveal turns on whether the contract fixed an order and, if not, on what the nature of the transaction requires under s 52.
modules.lab: runs twelve turns of a stalled project. The player is the contractor, caught between an owner who will not release the site until mobilisation is demonstrated and a supplier who will not deliver until paid. The physics is that s 51 lets a party withhold performance only where the counterparty is not ready and willing, so the game turns on establishing and documenting readiness, which costs money (mobilising equipment that may sit idle) and is the only thing that unlocks the counterparty's obligation. Three strategic layers operate together. First, the sequencing question under s 52: where the contract is silent, the nature of the transaction fixes the order, and the player can influence the characterisation by how they describe the works, which is the interpretive axis operating on performance rather than on words. Second, prevention under s 53: if the owner's failure to release the site is preventing performance, the contract becomes voidable at the contractor's option with compensation, which is a powerful weapon and a dangerous one, because exercising it ends the project and the contractor may prefer to be paid for building. Third, s 54, where the player's own default on a prior obligation destroys their claim on the dependent one and makes them liable, so the player must audit their own compliance before threatening anyone. Turn eight presents the decisive choice: with the project two months behind and the owner clearly in prevention, does the player elect to treat the contract as voidable and claim compensation, or affirm and continue building with a documented prevention claim reserved? Claude plays the owner with a policy of manufacturing readiness disputes to obscure its own prevention. Failure mode is a contractor who withholds performance to apply pressure, is found not to have been ready and willing, and converts a strong prevention claim into their own default under s 54.
modules.win_loss: Win by completing the project with a compensable prevention claim, or by electing to avoid at the point of maximum recovery. Lose instructively by withholding without documented readiness.
modules.build_notes: Dependency graph with per-obligation prerequisites. Readiness is a per-party score built from documented evidence actions and decaying without maintenance. Section 53 election must be a discrete branch with different endgames. Section 54 must automatically bar claims by a party in prior default on the prerequisite.

modules.title: Does delay terminate the contract or merely generate compensation?
modules.doctrine: Time as essence, non-essential delay and notice required when accepting late performance while claiming compensation.
modules.mechanic: manage wedding catering, commercial construction and commodity-delivery contracts with different sensitivity to time.
modules.authority: Hind Construction Contractors v State of Maharashtra, (1979) 2 SCC 70
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: identical two-week delays occur in all three contracts. The player predicts the consequence in each, and the reveal is that only one contract becomes voidable, which shows that the delay is not the operative fact.
modules.lab: manages all three contracts over six weeks with a limited management budget, so the player cannot attend to everything. The physics has two distinct stages. First, whether time is of the essence, which turns on the nature of the contract, the express terms and the surrounding circumstances rather than on the mere fixing of a date, and which the player can influence prospectively by making time expressly essential in writing, a move available in week one at a commercial cost because counterparties price it. Second, and this is the mechanic that catches almost every player, the notice requirement. When late performance is offered, the player must decide whether to accept, and if they accept they must give notice of their intention to claim compensation at that time. Accepting the catering delivery gratefully because the wedding is tomorrow, and raising the delay two weeks later, extinguishes the claim entirely. The game creates realistic pressure to accept without thinking: the caterer arrives late during the event, the construction contractor completes during a site visit, the commodity arrives when the player's own onward customer is waiting. Each is a moment where the commercially natural response destroys the legal one. Week five adds the reverse case, where the player has themselves performed late and must judge whether the counterparty's acceptance without notice has extinguished their exposure. Failure mode is a player who correctly identifies time as of the essence in the catering contract, accepts the late performance because they had no realistic alternative, and gives no notice.
modules.win_loss: Win by preserving compensation claims on all delayed contracts and correctly exercising or declining the voidability option. Lose instructively by accepting late performance without notice, which is the module's central trap and is entirely realistic.
modules.build_notes: essenceOfTime resolves from contractType, expressTerms and circumstances, with the Chand Rani presumption applied to immovable property. On acceptance of late performance, the notice check must fire immediately and silently disable the compensation claim if absent. Do not warn the player during play.

modules.title: Which of several debts did a payment discharge?
modules.doctrine: Appropriation by debtor, appropriation by creditor and statutory appropriation when neither acts.
modules.mechanic: distribute partial payments across debts with different dates, interest and limitation risks.
