modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a single payment is applied three ways and the player sees the very different resulting positions. The reveal is that s 60 lets the creditor apply a payment to a time-barred debt, which is the provision's most consequential feature and the one debtors most often overlook.
modules.lab: runs eight quarters from the debtor's chair. The player has limited cash each quarter and six debts, and must decide both how much to pay and how to appropriate it. The physics is that intimation at the time of payment is everything: an express intimation under s 59 binds the creditor, silence hands the option to the creditor under s 60, and if the creditor also stays silent the s 61 default applies payments in order of time, which may be the worst outcome of all where the oldest debt is unsecured and low-interest. The strategic problems compound. The player generally wants to protect secured debts and preserve the running of limitation on debts they hope will lapse, while the creditor (Claude, with a policy of appropriating to the debt closest to being time-barred and then to the least secured) wants the opposite. Quarter three introduces a payment made by a third party on the debtor's behalf, and the player must work out whose intimation counts. Quarter five introduces a guarantor whose exposure depends on which debt was discharged, so appropriation now affects a party outside the ledger, and the player's cheapest appropriation may destroy a relationship they need. Quarter seven presents a partial payment made under pressure with no time to compose an intimation, and the player must decide whether to send a written appropriation afterwards, which the game treats as ineffective because s 59 requires intimation at the time of payment or circumstances implying it, which is a strict rule and an instructive loss. Failure mode is a debtor who pays consistently and silently for two years and discovers that every rupee went to the debts they most wanted to lapse.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending eight quarters with the secured debts discharged and the intended debts time-barred. Lose instructively by paying without intimation, which quietly transfers the option to the creditor.
modules.build_notes: Each payment object requires an appropriation field set at payment time; later modification must be rejected with the statutory reason. Implement s 61 as the fallback in order of time with proportionate division for equal standing. Limitation clocks per debt, and a guarantor object whose exposure is derived from which debt is discharged.

modules.title: Can the parties replace, alter or end their contract?
modules.doctrine: Novation, alteration, consensual rescission and communication of rescission; distinguishing substitution from mere waiver.
modules.mechanic: change parties, prices and obligations and test whether the original contract survives.
modules.authority: Lata Construction v Dr Rameshchandra Ramniklal Shah, (2000) 1 SCC 586
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: three changes are proposed. Replacing the debtor, extending the tenor, and reducing one instalment. The player predicts the classification of each and the reveal shows that only the first discharged the guarantee.
modules.lab: runs a distressed restructuring across four rounds. The player acts for the lender and must restructure a facility that the borrower cannot service, while preserving the guarantee from the borrower's parent and the security over its receivables. The engine is that the changes that most help the borrower are the ones most likely to be characterised as novation, which discharges the guarantee, and the guarantee is the lender's principal protection. So the player must find changes that deliver relief without substituting a new contract. Extending time is a s 63 act by the promisee alone and does not require the borrower's agreement to be effective, but a generous extension may prejudice the guarantor's position. Substituting a group company as obligor is the borrower's preferred solution and is a textbook novation. Altering the interest basis is a variation that survives, but a sufficiently fundamental alteration may cross into substitution, and the game keeps that line genuinely uncertain rather than crisp, because it is uncertain. Claude plays the guarantor's counsel, whose entire strategy is to characterise whatever the lender agrees as a novation, and who will point to the parties' own documentation, so the way the restructuring is papered matters as much as its substance. Round three adds an accrued claim the lender wants to preserve, and the player must ensure the restructuring does not rescind the original contract in a way that takes the accrued right with it. Round four tests the result when the borrower fails again and the lender calls the guarantee. Failure mode is a lender who achieves an elegant restructuring, saves the borrower for two quarters, and finds the guarantee discharged when it matters.
modules.win_loss: Win by delivering enough relief to keep the borrower alive with the guarantee and security intact. Lose instructively by substituting the obligor, or by papering a variation in language that reads as substitution.
modules.build_notes: Classification resolves from a change vector (partyChange, obligationFundamentality, termChange) rather than from the label used. Guarantee and security objects hold discharge conditions triggered by novation. Accrued rights must be tracked separately and can be lost on rescission. Keep the fundamentality threshold visible as a band, not a line.

modules.title: Was performance impossible from the beginning or frustrated later?
modules.doctrine: Initial impossibility, supervening impossibility or unlawfulness, commercial hardship, self-induced events and restitution.
modules.mechanic: reveal destruction, legal prohibition, death, delay and cost escalation and decide whether the contract survives.
modules.authority: Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur & Co, AIR 1954 SC 44; Energy Watchdog v CERC, (2017) 14 SCC 80
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four events are dealt (destruction of the subject matter, a government prohibition, a fourfold rise in input costs, a six-month port closure). The player marks which frustrate the contract, and the reveal is that only two do, which is the practical-not-literal test in action.
modules.lab: runs the contract through eight events over five years, and the player must decide, event by event, whether to perform at rising cost, negotiate, or declare the contract void under s 56. The physics is that a wrong declaration is a repudiation, exposing the player to a damages claim, so the decision is a real gamble rather than a classification exercise. The Cost of Performance curve is deliberately seductive: it climbs steeply enough that walking away feels obviously right long before the law agrees. Three mechanics generate the depth. First, foreseeability and prevention: an event the promisor could have prevented, or which the contract allocated to them through a force majeure or price adjustment clause, does not frustrate, so the player's own drafting from earlier modules constrains them here. Second, self-induced frustration, where the player's decision to allocate scarce capacity to a more profitable customer creates their own impossibility, which the game models directly and which does not attract s 56. Third, the s 65 consequence: on frustration the contract becomes void and advantages received must be restored, and the player has received substantial advance payments, so a successful frustration claim triggers a large restitution obligation that may be worse than performing. That confrontation, which mirrors Module 36's, is the module's payoff. Round six presents the Satyabrata pattern precisely: a lengthy but temporary governmental requisition that makes performance impossible for now and not forever, and the player must decide whether the fundamental basis is destroyed. Failure mode is a player who declares frustration on the cost curve alone and faces both a damages claim and a restitution obligation.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending the five years with the best net position, whether by performing, renegotiating or correctly declaring the contract void. Lose instructively by declaring frustration on hardship, or by performing to ruin through an event that genuinely did frustrate.
modules.build_notes: Each event object carries foreseeable, preventable, unlawful, basisDestruction and costMultiplier. Frustration resolves on unlawful or basisDestruction only, never on costMultiplier, and the debrief must state this. Wrongful declaration must branch to a repudiation endgame. Section 65 restitution computes from advances and benefits received.

modules.title: Is this an actual breach or anticipatory repudiation?
modules.doctrine: Refusal or disabling performance, election to terminate or affirm, continued readiness and consequences of the election.
modules.mechanic: respond to cancellation messages, missed milestones and threatened non-performance before the due date.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four messages arrive and the player marks which constitute repudiation. The reveal is that the most alarming message (a threat to stop unless renegotiated) is a negotiating position and not a refusal in its entirety, while a quiet notice of a plant sale is a disabling act.
modules.lab: runs six weeks with a moving substitute market. The player is the buyer under a long-term supply contract, and the supplier's position deteriorates in a way that is ambiguous for several weeks before it becomes clear. The engine is that the election under s 39 is only available while the repudiation stands, and acquiescence by words or conduct destroys it, so continuing to place orders and accept partial deliveries may quietly affirm the contract, which is the same affirmation mechanic the player met in Module 4. The strategic problem is that the two branches have opposite market exposures. Terminating early crystallises the loss at today's substitute price and lets the player cover, which is right if prices are rising. Affirming keeps the contract alive at the contract price, which is right if prices are falling, but leaves the player holding the risk that the supplier fails completely and the player must then cover at whatever price prevails. Because the player does not know where prices are going, this is a genuine decision under uncertainty rather than a puzzle with an answer. Two further pressures apply. First, terminating on conduct that turns out not to be repudiation makes the player the repudiating party, which is catastrophic and which Claude's supplier will try to induce by sending pressure that stops just short of refusal. Second, s 73's mitigation principle (developed in Module 61) means that a player who affirms and does nothing may find their recoverable loss reduced anyway, so affirmation is not passive. Week five delivers an unambiguous repudiation, and the player's earlier conduct determines whether the election is still available. Failure mode is a buyer who keeps ordering to preserve goodwill and finds they have acquiesced.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending six weeks with supply secured at the best available net cost and the election exercised (or preserved) correctly. Lose instructively by terminating on a negotiating position, or by acquiescing into the loss of the election.
modules.build_notes: Each message is classified into refusal, disablement or neither by a resolver with reasons. An acquiescence tracker increments on orders placed and deliveries accepted after the repudiation. Price series is seeded and hidden. Wrongful termination must branch to the player becoming the defaulter.

modules.title: What position should damages place the claimant in?
modules.doctrine: Compensatory character, expectation and reliance measures, quantification and the rejection of ordinary punitive recovery.
modules.mechanic: reconstruct the claimant's position if the contract had been performed.
modules.authority: Murlidhar Chiranjilal v Harishchandra Dwarkadas, AIR 1962 SC 366
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a failed equipment delivery. The player builds a three-assumption counterfactual (the equipment would have worked, the factory would have run at capacity, the output would have sold at the current price) and sees the claim value and then the evidential fragility of the third assumption.
modules.lab: is a quantification exercise with an evidence budget across four heads of loss. The physics is that every additional assumption in the counterfactual increases the claim's value and decreases its probability, since the chain is only as strong as its weakest link, so the player must find the point at which extending the chain stops paying. This is the module's core insight and it is rarely taught explicitly. The strategic decisions run as follows. First, expectation or reliance: expectation puts the claimant where performance would have left them and is worth more, but requires proving the counterfactual; reliance recovers what was spent in reliance and requires proving only expenditure, which is far easier but caps recovery, and is the right answer where the venture's profitability was speculative. The player must choose, and choosing wrongly for a speculative venture is a classic and expensive error. Second, which heads to pursue, since the evidence budget cannot cover all four, and the most valuable head is usually the least provable. Third, whether to plead in the alternative, which the game permits at a credibility cost because pleading reliance alongside expectation signals doubt about the counterfactual, and Claude will say so. Round three introduces a documentary discovery that either supports or destroys the central assumption, and the player's earlier budget allocation determines whether they find it in time. Round four applies the Explanation's requirement that the means available for remedying the inconvenience be taken into account, which reduces the claim by whatever the player could have done and did not, connecting forward to Module 61. Failure mode is a magnificent expectation claim resting on a five-link chain, of which the counterparty breaks link four.
modules.win_loss: Win by recovering the highest expected value, computed as claim value multiplied by probability. Lose instructively by maximising claim value at the cost of provability, or by choosing reliance for a venture whose profitability was demonstrable.
modules.build_notes: Counterfactual is a chain of assumption objects, each with value contribution and probability. Claim expected value is the product of probabilities times the value gap, and must be shown live so the trade-off is legible. Include a culpability attribute on the defendant that is deliberately wired to affect nothing.

modules.title: Is the claimed loss caused, foreseeable and reasonably avoidable?
modules.doctrine: Causation, ordinary-course loss, contemplation of parties, remote or indirect loss and mitigation.
modules.mechanic: pass each claimed loss through causation, remoteness, proof and mitigation filters.
modules.authority: Murlidhar Chiranjilal v Harishchandra Dwarkadas, AIR 1962 SC 366
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: one loss of a very large downstream contract is put through the pipeline and emerges tiny, because the supplier never knew about the downstream contract. The reveal is that the decisive fact was communicated (or not) at the time of contracting, long before the breach.
modules.lab: is played in two time zones, which is what makes it more than a filtering drill. The first half is set before any breach: the player is negotiating a supply contract and must decide how much to tell the supplier about their special circumstances. Disclosing that a late delivery will cost them a lucrative downstream contract brings that loss within the parties' knowledge and makes it recoverable, but the supplier will price the risk, demand a liability cap (which is Module 50's territory) or decline the business. Staying quiet keeps the price low and caps the player's recovery at ordinary loss. This is a real commercial trade-off and most players get it wrong in one direction or the other. The second half is set immediately after breach, and the mitigation filter dominates. The player has a limited window and several options: cover at a high price now, wait for a better price, repair, or do nothing and claim. The Explanation requires that available means of remedying the inconvenience be taken into account, so doing nothing reduces the recoverable loss by what reasonable action would have saved, and the game applies that reduction without mercy. But mitigation is costly and uncertain, and covering at a panic price may itself be unreasonable, so the player must judge what a reasonable person would have done, not what turned out best. Round three reveals the counterfactual market so the player can see whether their mitigation was reasonable in hindsight, and the debrief makes the point that the test is not hindsight. Round four introduces a loss that was caused by the breach and by an independent event, testing the causation filter directly. Failure mode is a player who says nothing at contracting, mitigates poorly, and recovers a fraction of a substantial loss.
modules.win_loss: Win by maximising net recovery across both halves, accounting for the price paid at contracting for the disclosure. Lose instructively by disclosing everything and paying a premium for a risk that never materialises, or by disclosing nothing and losing the downstream claim.
modules.build_notes: Four sequential filter functions applied per head of loss, each reporting the amount removed and why. Disclosure at contracting sets a knowledge flag that the second filter reads. Mitigation reasonableness must be judged against information available at the time, not outcomes, and the debrief should show both.

modules.title: Does the amount written into the contract control compensation?
modules.doctrine: Reasonable compensation up to the stipulated sum, penalty clauses, liquidated amounts, forfeiture and proof of loss.
modules.mechanic: draft a clause and run minor, serious and technically provable breaches through it.
modules.authority: Fateh Chand v Balkishan Dass, AIR 1963 SC 1405; Kailash Nath Associates v DDA, (2015) 4 SCC 136
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player is shown a clause stipulating ten lakh rupees for any delay and three breaches (one day with no effect, a serious delay, and a breach after which the buyer profited). They predict the recovery in each, and the reveal is that the named sum is a ceiling and that the third breach may yield nothing at all.
modules.lab: has two phases. Phase one is drafting, with four decisions and no dominant move. The number itself: because s 74 makes the sum a ceiling, a high figure buys nothing on the upside and invites the court to read it down, while a modest figure permanently caps recovery even where real loss runs far beyond it. The structure: forfeiture of money already held versus a sum payable on breach, since money in hand reverses who must sue and who must prove, though Kailash Nath applies s 74 scrutiny to forfeiture too and adds an arbitrariness constraint against a public authority. The evidentiary architecture: the player may spend bargaining budget embedding a recital of how the figure was calculated, which is the only move that hedges against a judge on the Kailash Nath line, because it lets the clause carry part of its own proof. And whether to make the sum the exclusive remedy, which feels like risk control but, under SRA s 23, surrenders specific performance if the sum reads as being in lieu of performance, and this contract has one component the buyer cannot source elsewhere. Phase two runs the clause through three escalating breaches, before a judge drawn at random from the Saw Pipes line or the Kailash Nath line, whose identity the player does not learn until after the draft is locked. A one-day delay with no material effect, where invoking the clause is legally available and strategically ruinous because it hands the opponent the penalty argument. A serious delay whose loss is genuine but awkward to quantify, which is the Saw Pipes zone and where the recital either saves the player or does not exist. And a breach where the supplier's default coincided with a market movement that left the buyer better off, which is the Kailash Nath fact pattern, no loss, and the ceiling collapses to nothing. Claude plays opposing counsel, attacking whichever limb the drafter left weakest and characterising a high number as a penalty. The failure modes are instructive rather than punitive: a clause read down to nil for want of loss, a ceiling capping a claim below actual damage, and exclusivity drafting that quietly extinguishes specific performance over the one asset that mattered.
modules.win_loss: Win by carrying the highest aggregate recovery across all three breaches while retaining specific performance over the critical component, under a judge whose doctrinal line the player did not choose. Lose instructively by drafting a clause that wins spectacularly under one line and returns nothing under the other, which teaches that s 74 drafting is risk allocation under interpretive uncertainty rather than arithmetic.
modules.build_notes: The judge is drawn from two policy objects (proofRequired true or false) after the draft locks. Recovery resolves as min(stipulatedSum, reasonableCompensation), with reasonableCompensation dependent on provableLoss and, under the Saw Pipes policy, on preEstimateRecitalStrength where proof is difficult. SRA s 23 exposure is a separate boolean derived from exclusivity drafting and must gate specific performance independently of the damages computation.

modules.title: Should the claimant demand performance, replacement performance or money?
modules.doctrine: Post-2018 specific performance, statutory bars, readiness and willingness, substituted performance, notice and compensation.
modules.mechanic: choose between waiting, issuing a thirty-day notice, hiring a substitute and suing for performance or damages.
modules.authority: Katta Sujatha Reddy v Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt Ltd, (2023) 1 SCC 355
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player picks a route without knowing the interaction rules and discovers that procuring substituted performance under s 20 closed the specific performance route under ss 14 and 16. The reveal is the interlock between the sections.
modules.lab: runs a twelve-week decision under commercial pressure. The player needs the asset, the defaulting seller is stalling, substitution costs rise weekly as the market tightens, and litigation is slow. The physics is the interlock: the routes are not parallel options but a decision tree in which early moves prune later branches. Serving the s 20 notice starts a thirty-day clock that costs nothing to start and preserves optionality, which most players discover too late to use. Three decisions carry the game. First, whether to serve the notice immediately, which is cheap and preserves the substitution route without committing to it, against the risk that it signals to the seller that the buyer will not seek performance. Second, whether to maintain readiness and willingness, which s 16 requires for specific performance and which costs money (keeping funds available, continuing to perform the buyer's own obligations) even while the seller is in default, and which Module 54 has already trained the player to document. Third, the timing of substitution: substituting early caps the cost but forecloses specific performance permanently under ss 14 and 16, and the asset is bespoke, so the substitute is imperfect. Claude plays the seller with a policy of stalling just enough to run the clock while occasionally signalling willingness, precisely to keep the buyer from committing to a route. Week nine introduces a third party who offers to buy the asset from the seller, which threatens the specific performance route entirely and forces a decision. Failure mode is a buyer who waits for performance, maintains readiness impeccably, and finds at week twelve that substitution now costs three times what it did in week two.
modules.win_loss: Win by obtaining the asset or its economic equivalent at the lowest net cost including delay. Lose instructively by procuring substitution and then discovering the seller would have performed, or by holding out for specific performance while the substitution market moves away.
modules.build_notes: Implement route availability as a state machine where s 20 substitution sets specificPerformanceAvailable to false via ss 14 and 16. Readiness and willingness is a maintained score with an ongoing cost. Substitution cost is a rising series. The thirty-day notice must be startable without committing, since that optionality is the key teaching point.

modules.title: Which corrective or preventive remedy fits the problem?
modules.doctrine: Rectification, rescission, cancellation, injunction, restoration and compensation; compatibility between remedies.
modules.mechanic: plead with a limited hand of remedy cards and lose relief when incompatible remedies are combined.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player pleads rescission and rectification together and the hand rejects the combination, because rectification affirms the instrument while rescission unmakes it. The reveal is that remedies encode inconsistent theories of the transaction.
modules.lab: is a full pleading and relief exercise across a dispute with several strands: an instrument that misstates the agreed boundary, a contract induced by misrepresentation, a negative covenant the defendant is breaching, and benefits that have passed both ways. The player must select and sequence relief, and the game enforces coherence strictly, because inconsistent relief is the most common failure in real pleadings and the most invisible in teaching materials. The decisions build on each other. Rectification and rescission are mutually exclusive on the same instrument, so the player must decide whether their client's story is that the document is wrong (rectify and then enforce) or that the transaction should never have happened (rescind and restore). Injunctive relief under ss 36 to 42 requires the player to consider whether damages would be adequate, and s 40's power to award damages in lieu means the player may win the argument and receive money rather than the injunction, which is a real risk where the client wants the behaviour stopped. Restoration under ss 30 and 33 and under ICA ss 64 and 65 attaches to rescission and cancellation, so the player must compute what their own client will have to give back, which mirrors the lesson from Modules 36 and 58. Round three introduces the client's actual priority, discoverable only by asking, and it turns out to be stopping the defendant's conduct rather than unwinding the transaction, which makes the injunction the centre of the case and demotes everything else. Round four is the hearing, where Claude, as the bench, tests the coherence of the combination and refuses relief that contradicts other relief sought. Failure mode is a player who pleads comprehensively, is met with the observation that they cannot both affirm and disaffirm, and is put to an election at the worst moment.
modules.win_loss: Win by obtaining a coherent package that delivers the client's actual priority. Lose instructively by pleading incompatible relief, or by winning rescission for a client who needed an injunction.
modules.build_notes: Encode remedies as objects with prerequisites and an incompatibility matrix. Coherence is checked across the selected set and must name the specific contradiction. Section 40 damages in lieu should fire probabilistically where damages would be adequate, so the injunction is never a certainty. Client priority is discoverable only through an interview action.

modules.title: Can a person who was not a contracting party sue on the promise?
modules.anchor: ICA ss 2(d), 2(h), 73; SRA s 15(a); case law
modules.doctrine: Privity of contract versus the Indian rule that consideration may move from another person.
modules.mechanic: map promisor, promisee, provider of consideration and beneficiary and identify who possesses an enforceable right.
modules.authority: M C Chacko v State Bank of Travancore, (1969) 2 SCC 343
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: an arrangement in which a father pays a builder to construct a house for his daughter. The player marks whether consideration exists and who can sue if the builder fails. The reveal is that consideration is fine, the daughter cannot sue, and the father can, which surprises almost everyone.
modules.lab: is a structuring engagement with a hard constraint. The player advises a family business setting up a series of arrangements for the benefit of persons who will not be signing anything: an elderly parent to be maintained, a sibling to receive a share of proceeds, and a dependent to be paid an allowance. In each case the person with the strongest interest in performance is the person least able to enforce it, which is the practical problem privity creates and which the module exists to solve. The available moves are the structural answers. Making the beneficiary a party to the contract is the simplest and often the most resisted, since the family may not want the dependent involved in negotiations, and Claude, playing the family principal, resists it for exactly those reasons, forcing the player to argue for it commercially rather than legally. Creating a trust over the contractual right is the classic route recognised in Chacko and points forward to Module 66, but it requires a genuine intention to create a trust rather than a mere intention to benefit, which the game tests strictly. Structuring as a family arrangement brings the second Chacko exception into play but requires the hallmarks of such an arrangement. A fourth move, giving the promisee a strong incentive to enforce (for instance by making the promisee liable to the beneficiary independently), works without any exception at all and is frequently the cheapest answer, and the game rewards players who find it. Round three tests the structures by having the promisor default and each intended beneficiary attempt to enforce, and the player watches which of their structures actually produced standing. Failure mode is a structure in which every promise is supported by consideration under s 2(d) and no beneficiary can sue, which is precisely the trap the Indian rule sets.
modules.win_loss: Win by producing structures in which each intended beneficiary can enforce, directly or through a party with a genuine incentive. Lose instructively by relying on s 2(d) as if it solved privity, which is the module's target misconception.
modules.build_notes: Two independent resolvers over the same graph, considerationSatisfied and hasStanding, rendered as separate indicators that must never be combined. Standing resolves true only for parties, trust beneficiaries and family arrangement participants. The incentive route works by making the promisee a claimant, not the beneficiary.

modules.title: When may a third-party beneficiary nevertheless enforce the arrangement?
modules.anchor: SRA ss 11, 15, 19; Indian Trusts Act ss 56, 59; TPA s 40; case law
modules.doctrine: Trust or charge, marriage and family arrangements, acknowledgment and estoppel; agency and assignment remain excluded.
modules.mechanic: the beneficiary must produce the elements of a recognized exception before entering the enforcement forum.
modules.authority: Khwaja Muhammad Khan v Husaini Begum, (1910) 37 IA 152; M C Chacko v State Bank of Travancore, (1969) 2 SCC 343
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: a beneficiary approaches all four gates with the same facts and passes none, then acquires one further fact (a clause charging identified property) and passes one. The reveal is that the exceptions are element-based rather than merit-based.
modules.lab: is a two-stage exercise, drafting then enforcing, which is the only honest way to teach these exceptions because they are almost always won or lost at drafting. In stage one the player drafts a maintenance arrangement in a family settlement, choosing how far to go: expressing an intention to create a trust (strong, and it constrains the promisor's flexibility, which the family resists), charging identified property (strong, and it encumbers an asset the family wants free), or relying on the family arrangement character alone (cheap, and it depends on the arrangement having the right hallmarks). Each choice costs family goodwill, which is a modelled resource because these arrangements are negotiated among people who must continue to live together. In stage two the promisor defaults years later, and the beneficiary, now the player's client, must get through a gate. The physics is strict element-checking, and the game refuses partial credit: an intention to benefit is not an intention to create a trust, and the distinction is exactly what Chacko turned on. Claude plays the promisor's counsel, whose policy is to concede the moral position freely and attack the missing element, which teaches the player that sympathy does not open gates. Round three introduces an acknowledgment made by the promisor during the intervening years, and the player must decide whether to build the case on that acknowledgment (available, fact-dependent, and it does not require anything from the original drafting) or on the drafted route, which is a genuine strategic choice with different evidence requirements. Failure mode is a beneficiary with an unimpeachable moral claim, a clearly expressed intention that they should benefit, and no stamp for any gate.
modules.win_loss: Win by passing at least one gate. Lose instructively by relying on the strength of the intention to benefit, which is precisely what the exceptions do not require and do not accept.
modules.build_notes: Each gate is a conjunctive stamp checker naming the missing element. Trust intention must be a distinct attribute from benefitIntention, and the interface should let the player see them as separate fields. Family goodwill is a resource consumed by protective drafting. The acknowledgment route must be available independently of stage one.

modules.title: Must benefits be returned when a transaction is rescinded or becomes void?
modules.doctrine: Restitution following rescission of a voidable contract versus restoration under a void agreement or contract that later becomes void.
modules.mechanic: reverse payments, property transfers and consumed benefits while calculating possible compensation.
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player rescinds a transaction and the ledger runs. The reveal is that the client, having consumed and improved what they received, ends up paying to escape, which is counter-intuitive and is the module's whole point.
modules.lab: runs three parallel unwindings with different legal characters, which forces the player to track the doctrinal routes rather than treating restitution as one rule. The first is a voidable contract the client wishes to rescind under s 19, where s 64 requires the rescinding party to restore benefits received. The second is an agreement discovered to be void, where s 65 obliges any person who received an advantage to restore it, so the obligation runs both ways and does not depend on who wants out. The third is a contract that becomes void under s 56, where s 65 applies to advantages received before frustration and the timing of receipt matters. The strategy sits in preparation and sequencing. The player has four preparatory moves available before initiating any unwinding: valuing benefits at receipt (which fixes the measure favourably if values have since risen), documenting consumption (which converts an in-specie restoration into a compensation claim the player may prefer), segregating what has been received so it survives in identifiable form, and dealing with a third party who acquired part of the property. Each move costs time, and the counterparty's position deteriorates during the delay, so waiting is not free. Round three introduces SRA ss 30 and 33, where the court may impose restoration as a condition of granting relief, which means the player may be ordered to restore more than s 64 alone would require, and the player must decide whether to seek court-ordered rescission (cleaner, conditional) or to rescind by notice and litigate afterwards. Failure mode is a client who rescinds enthusiastically, restores everything at present values, and would have been better off performing.
modules.win_loss: Win by achieving the best Net Position across the three unwindings. Lose instructively by unwinding a transaction whose restitution cost exceeds the benefit of escape, which is the commonest real-world error in rescission advice.
modules.build_notes: Restitution ledger with per-benefit valueAtReceipt, valueNow, survivesInSpecie and thirdPartyInterest. Section 64 applies only to the rescinding party's restoration; s 65 applies to any person who received an advantage. SRA ss 30 and 33 add a court-imposed condition layer available only on the court route.

modules.title: Can a useful act create an obligation without an agreement?
modules.doctrine: Interested payment of another's legal liability and lawful non-gratuitous acts whose benefits are enjoyed.
modules.mechanic: decide who must reimburse taxes, emergency repairs and unsolicited but knowingly accepted services.
modules.authority: State of West Bengal v B K Mondal & Sons, AIR 1962 SC 779
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: four acts are tested. The reveal is that two fail, one because the beneficiary never enjoyed the benefit and one because the act was done as a neighbourly favour, which negatives the non-gratuitous element that s 70 requires.
modules.lab: runs a year in the complex from the position of a resident who keeps having to act because others will not. Each month presents a decision: act or not, and if acting, how to act in a way that will support a claim. The physics is that ss 69 and 70 have different element sets and the player must choose which they are building toward before acting, because the evidence differs. Section 69 requires that someone else was bound by law to pay and that the player had an interest in making the payment, which is easy to satisfy for municipal taxes on a co-owned property and impossible for a voluntary contribution to a neighbour's private repair. Section 70 requires a lawful act, a non-gratuitous intention, and enjoyment of the benefit by the other. The interesting decisions are social as well as legal. Announcing in advance that the player expects reimbursement establishes the non-gratuitous intention and poisons the relationship, and the game models neighbour goodwill as a resource with real consequences, since the player needs cooperation for later acts. Staying silent preserves goodwill and risks the claim being characterised as a favour, which is the most common way s 70 claims fail. A middle path, a written note to the association recording the expectation of contribution without confronting individuals, is available and is the answer most players eventually find. Two further wrinkles: in one month the beneficiary expressly refuses the service before it is rendered and then benefits from it anyway, which raises the question whether enjoyment of the benefit was voluntary, and in another the act turns out to be unlawful (work done without a required permission), which closes s 70 entirely regardless of benefit. Failure mode is a helpful resident who spends a year improving the complex and recovers nothing because every act looked gratuitous.
modules.win_loss: Win by ending the year with reimbursement above threshold and goodwill above the floor. Lose instructively by acting generously and silently, which is admirable and legally worthless.
modules.build_notes: Two element checkers, one per section, run against each act object. nonGratuitousIntent must be set by a player action taken before or at the time of the act, never afterwards. Goodwill is a resource affected by how the intention is externalised. Include an unlawful act that closes s 70 irrespective of benefit.

modules.title: Must money or property transferred by mistake or coercion be restored?
modules.doctrine: Scope of mistake and coercion, restitution of duplicate or erroneous payments and defences developed through case law.
modules.mechanic: investigate duplicate transfers, mistaken tax payments and payments made under unlawful pressure.
modules.authority: Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v Kanhaiya Lal Mukundlal Saraf, AIR 1959 SC 135
modules.core: Five-minute ramp: the player attempts recovery on three transfers and the reveal is that the mistake-of-law payment is recoverable, which contradicts the intuition most learners take from s 21, and that the payment made with full knowledge is not a mistake at all.
modules.lab: runs a recovery programme across four quarters with a litigation budget. The physics is that s 72 states a broad rule and the contest happens in the defences, so the player's real work is anticipatory. Limitation runs from a point that depends on when the mistake was discovered, so the tax claim's viability turns on when the invalidity became known, and investigating that costs a move. Recipients who have changed their position in reliance on the receipt present a harder claim, and the player must decide whether to pursue quickly (before positions change further) or thoroughly (with better evidence). Three decisions shape the programme. First, sequencing: the duplicate payment is easy and small, the tax claim is large and slow, and the coerced payment depends on establishing that the detention was unlawful, which is Module 30's work and which the player must fund. Second, characterisation: the payment made under protest with full knowledge is not recoverable as a mistake, so the player must run it as coercion or not at all, and the quality of the protest record determines whether that is possible, which retrospectively justifies the discipline taught in Module 30. Third, the counterparty relationship, since the vendor who received the duplicate payment is a continuing supplier and an aggressive claim costs commercial value, so the player must weigh recovery against relationship. Quarter three introduces a recipient who has distributed the money onward, raising the question of how far s 72 reaches, which the game presents as an open area with a range of outcomes rather than a settled rule. Failure mode is a finance function that discovers all five transfers in quarter one, litigates them in order of size, and finds the two small easy ones time-barred by the time it reaches them.
modules.win_loss: Win by recovering above the target across the four quarters within budget and without losing the key supplier relationship. Lose instructively by characterising a knowing payment as a mistake, or by letting limitation run on the easy claims while pursuing the hard one.
modules.build_notes: Each transfer object holds transferBasis (mistakeOfFact, mistakeOfLaw, coercion, knowingPayment), discoveryDate, and recipientPositionChange. Limitation runs from discoveryDate. Knowing payments must fail the mistake route and be routed to coercion only where a protest record exists. Present the onward-distribution question as a range of outcomes with the uncertainty stated.
